The Soccer Saturday legend on his remarkable 2026 journey from Borneo, and the most disastrous choice he could have made for a travel partner...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jeff Stelling hosted Soccer Saturday for 29 years between 1994 and 2023 – but the end of his tenure has given him the opportunity to explore the world this year.

Stelling is currently starring in BBC One show Celebrity Race Across The World, having recently travelled from Borneo to Malaysia alongside his son Matt.

The rules of the expedition, however, meant Stelling wasn’t allowed to contact home or find out the scores of his beloved Hartlepool United.

Among the competition in the other three pairs were singers Sam Ryder and Ella Eyre, plus the offspring of Katie Price and Peter Andre, although Stelling admits to FourFourTwo that the show wasn’t exactly relaxed.

“It was incredibly stressful, because you’ve got no phone, you can’t find the football scores – no credit cards, £26 a day between the two of you for transport, food and accommodation, and you find yourself sleeping on floors, surrounded by rats in some cases,” he told us.

“But you see the most incredible sights, things I didn’t know existed. It was an amazing experience.”

Even in the remote north of Australia, Stelling still heard the familiar catchphrase of 'Unbelievable, Jeff!' – once coined by his Soccer Saturday pal Chris Kamara.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Wherever I go, someone will shout it and laugh as if it’s the first time it’s ever been done…” Stelling smiles – in this week’s episode, it was clear that hearing the catchphrase cheered him up, after a tough few days of travelling.

“It became part of football terminology – could you believe from the beginnings of Soccer Saturday that, 30 years later, people still use it? When I was in Australia, a gang of guys outside a hostel shouted it.”

Stelling travelled with his son on this occasion, having previously ventured to far-flung places with Kamara – heading to Sri Lanka on World’s Most Dangerous Roads.

If he’d had to choose a former footballer to travel with for Celebrity Race Across The World, who would have been the worst person he could have chosen?

“Oh, Gabby Agbonlahor,” Stelling replies instantly with a laugh, referencing his talkSPORT colleague. “His geographical knowledge isn’t quite of the standard required. He couldn’t do Race Across Birmingham!”

Stelling was speaking to FFT at the home of Woking FC as part of National League’s title sponsor Enterprise’s Local Legends campaign.

Nominations are being invited for unsung heroes across the league’s three divisions, with six eventually chosen to have their faces displayed on Wembley Way on National League play-off final weekend in May. Enterprise will also donate to community or charitable initiatives of all six associated clubs.

“In the National League, and National League North and South, virtually every club is the heartbeat of the community – there’s no other occasion when so many people from different walks of life within that community will be together,” says Stelling, whose boyhood club returned to the National League in 2023.

“Watching Hartlepool isn’t always therapeutic, but there’s nothing bigger in the community than Hartlepool United.

“For clubs like us, when the good times are so few and far between, you remember them far better. When we won promotion from the National League to the Football League in 2021, it was one of the greatest days of my life.”

There will be more from Stelling on his career in football in the next issue of FourFourTwo magazine.

Jeff Stelling has launched Enterprise’s search for the National League’s Local Legends – celebrating those who turn up for their club and community week in, week out. Click here to nominate.

#966. How West Ham striker's testicular cancer tragedy is educating next generation

Mother and brother of former West Ham and Australia youth team striker Dylan Tombides have partnered with FIFA to raise awareness of testicular cancer; Visit dt38.org to find out more about DT38 Foundation, Dylan's story and advice and guidance about testicular cancer.

Senior Football Journalist @psmithXI

Fifteen years on from West Ham striker Dylan Tombides discovering he had testicular cancer at the U17 World Cup, his mother and brother are back at the tournament delivering inspiring, emotional talks to the current generation of players to raise awareness in his honour.

Tombides passed away in April 2014 aged just 20, following a battle with the cancer he was diagnosed with while on international duty with Australia's youth team in Mexico in 2011.

A random drugs test revealed what had originally been misdiagnosed by his GP as a cyst was far more serious. Three years of "really intense chemotherapy" followed, says his mother Tracy.

The DT38 Foundation was set up in his name and, in partnership with FIFA Medical, Tracy and Dylan's brother Taylor are part of the initiative at this year's tournament in Doha to explain to players why regular self-examination matters and how to carry it out.

"Getting the call from FIFA was a massive opportunity and an amazing thing for us and for the charity," says Taylor. "Obviously, it's where Dylan last kind of played healthy before his diagnosis. So to come back to where it all started for us as a family is a grateful honour."

During two weeks of talks to 48 teams, Tracy and Taylor have presented to 1,200 players.

With testicular cancer the most common cancer in males aged 15 to 44 - but highly treatable and in most cases curable when detected early - the importance of the sessions could be life changing.

"It's the number one cause of fatality of cancer in this particular age group," explains Dr Andy Massey, FIFA's Medical Director, who helped form the partnership and has overseen the provision of free scans to players during the tournament.

"This is one of the biggest things I think I've ever done in my sports medicine career because it has such a reach."

Tracy and Taylor's accounts of Dylan's stories have had a powerful impact on their audiences.

"One of the young players stood in front of me and said, 'I'm so sorry for your loss. I'm sorry your son isn't coming home to you. We are so grateful that you are telling us all about it'," says Tracy, recounting a talk with the Jamaican team. A similarly emotional conversation with the French squad ended in hugs instead of handshakes.

The DT38 Foundation have a campaign called Check One Two, encouraging men to check themselves on the first day of every month. Dylan's nickname 'Didge' also provides an acronym and hashtag for the foundation: Delay Is Deadly, Get Educated.

"Early detection is the difference between dealing with cancer treatment that has a 96 per cent cure rate or the figures drop away very, very quickly if you have to go to round two or round three of chemotherapy," says Tracy, who also encourages men with concerns to "insist on an ultrasound" test.

Tracy and Taylor treasure "messages that we've got from people who say, 'I thought of Dylan's story when I found a lump and I knew not to delay. I had testicular cancer and now I'm cancer-free and Dylan saved my life'."

"That tells us that what we're doing is life-changing for that family, that person," says Tracy.

Taylor believes they can have an impact through generations, too. "The effect is lasting. If we can teach these kids now, we know the next generation, they'll teach their kids and they'll teach their kids and it'll be continuous," he says.

"We're not just affecting one life, we're affecting a whole generation of lives, which is the biggest part of it. Without FIFA, we couldn't touch as many people as we have."

Visit dt38.org to find out more about the DT38 Foundation, Dylan's story and advice and guidance about testicular cancer.

Arsenal are causing a “transfer frenzy” in South America, over a highly-rated wonderkid.

That's according to a new report that says that the Premier League champions are looking to improve their squad over the long term, as much as they are interested in adding players who can help the team fight on three fronts.

FourFourTwo understands that manager Mikel Arteta is keen to add dynamic difference makers in attack – but Arsenal could well surprise everyone by adding a 19-year-old who isn't well-known to Premier League fans.

During Arteta's early tenure as manager, the Gunners leant into the South American market, bringing in Pablo Mari from Flamengo as the Basque boss's first signing, six months after landing Gabriel Martinelli from the fourth tier of Brazilian football.

Since then, Arteta has built around the likes of Gabriel Jesus and Gabriel Magalhaes, while bringing in Argentine assistant Gabriel Heinze.

#964. ‘I cannot sleep!’: Mauricio Pochettino speaks in Man United press conference - latest updates

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino has replaced Michael Carrick as United’s head coach and will lead the team in his first match against Liverpool on Sunday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino joked he “cannot sleep” as he bids to turn Manchester United’s fortunes around, having only managed a few hours per night as he faces a rapid turnaround since landing into the job on Wednesday.

Pochettino flew straight to Manchester after concluding his time with the United States and immediately met with his players as he aims to get to grips with the squad ahead of a crucial clash with Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

The task facing Pochettino is clear as he inherits a United team that will go into the weekend 18th in the table, following the dismissal of Michael Carrick last week, and the former Tottenham boss insisted his players understand that drastic improvement is needed.

“I think the culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear,” said Pochettino, who confirmed that Bruno Fernandes will remain his captain. “It's an historic club with amazing years of competing and being one of the best clubs in the world.

"It's difficult to find another club the size of club that is Manchester United, and I think is what we need to do is to be very open-minded and try to do our best to try to perform, and to that the players need to buy into the idea of that we need to improve.

"That is our job. After a few days of work, the job is to try to find a way to perform on Sunday and start to get the result that that club historically needs, and it's because Manchester United needs to be in a place in a different place than we are now."

Follow all the updates from Pochettino’s first press conference with our live blog below:

Mauricio Pochettino was asked about Bruno Fernandes and whether he will remain captain of Manchester United.

Fernandes has been outspoken this season, especially concerning tactics from former boss Michael Carrick, and is yet to agree a new deal with the club.

Pochettino confirmed that Fernandes would remain as captain but stressed that other players in the squad need to feel important to the team as well.

Mauricio Pochettino prefers a high-octane style of football, although that could prove difficult at Old Trafford with Man United’s running numbers among the worst in the league.

Manchester United will not pursue legal proceedings following the publication of unauthorised drone footage showing Mauricio Pochettino leading his first training session as head coach.

A 12-minute video was published online after a drone operator flew close to the club’s Carrington training complex on Thursday.

So, there ends Mauricio Pochettino’s first press conference as Manchester United’s head coach.

Plenty of questions about his journey to Old Trafford, how he plans to lead the club and how he’s settled in.

Not much focus on the Liverpool game though Pochettino confirmed that he and his squad at 100% focused on performing well at Anfield.

“You never know,” Pochettino said when asked if this was the right time for him to join United having previously missed out on the head coach role.

“You never know because timing is timing and football manages the timing.

“You never know when the time will come and the opportunity. I think we were prepared. We were ready if a club like Manchester United happened, you cannot turn it down.”

"We were missing a lot,” Pochettino said of the routine of club football.

“We are animals of the grass. We like to feel and smell the grass. To try and feel the players improve everyday.

“It’s a different job at the national team, at the same time you learn a lot and I think we are much better coaches."

When asked how the grass smells at Carrington, Pochettino replied:

“Lovely. Yesterday it rained and today it was sunny, it was a lovely morning."

Pochettino was asked what his message to the fans is at the start of his tenure.

“After two days, we expect the fans to be with us. But anything they can express I think we are going to be very emphatic with them.”

"When we arrive, I think we found a group of players that we propose to do the football that we feel,” Pochettino said.

“To be brave and be Manchester United. It is about proposing that idea to be brave and take it to the field.

"We cannot talk about things without context. And data is without context.

“It is easy to manipulate data but it is true and we need to be honest sometimes data show something that you can see on the field.

“We will try to improve our data in every single area of the field. We are here not to denounce things. We are here to build something with our players and with the club and try to perform and win games."

“When you don’t win games it’s normal that the confidence goes down,” Pochettino said.

"I think the players need to feel from us that you believe and trust in them, and show that you know what you are doing. That is important thing.

“I think the reception and the welcome in the last two days has been good.

"With the schedule we have ahead we have to settle on our principles. The players are intelligent, they have quality. It is something to unlock.

"Sometimes it is unlocking some things that didn't appear for different reasons."

“Experience is an important thing,” Pochettino said.

“To learn from experiences is amazing. I think we are much better coaches now having worked with a national team like USA because the expectation and pressure was massive.

“I don’t know, it own first game against Paraquay the pressure was massive. Expecting us to win and play well, all the country was behind us.

“When you are in Premier League, LaLiga or in France you feel the pressure but being there [at the World Cup] was massive pressure.

“We learn how to transform that pressure and use it. We need to find the right way to operate at the club and provide a platform to perform.”

Former striker assesses how many caps he could have reached, had he been able to continue playing regularly at club level

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Harry Kane is England’s new leading appearance-maker after passing Peter Shilton’s record last week – and he hasn’t been the only player tipped to reach the milestone over the years.

Shilton’s record of 125 Three Lions caps had stood since he made his final appearance for his country at the 1990 World Cup, before Kane played his 126th cap against Croatia, then made it 127 against Spain on Sunday.

Wayne Rooney had previously finished agonisingly short on 120, with David Beckham winning 115 caps, Steven Gerrard reaching 114, Ashley Cole making it to 107 and Frank Lampard clocking up 106.

Another player who looked on course to surpass Shilton at one point was Michael Owen, who won his 89th cap at the age of just 28, but didn’t add to his tally as injuries derailed his career.

Asked whether he feels he would have made it to 126 if the injuries hadn’t hit, the former striker is philosophical about it.

“I’m not that bothered about that, I had my time,” he told FFT. “In little moments when you think back over your career, you think of things, but that’s across the board, isn’t it?

“If I didn’t get injured then, would I have won more Golden Boots? Would I have won the Ballon d’Or more? Would I have won more of anything? You just never know. It’s one of those things.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“There’s no question about it, if I had Harry Kane’s constitution, there’s no doubt I would have scored many, many, many more goals than I did, played many, many, many more games than I did, and all the rest of it.

“But I’m happy with my lot, I played 89 times for England – that’s quite a lot. That’s just life, isn’t it? You can’t spend your life thinking ‘What if?’”

Owen reserved praise for Kane, who has scored an incredible 93 goals during his 127 caps.

“What he’s done is extraordinary really,” Owen said, speaking in association with soccer betting odds. “He’s fine-tuned his game to become one of the most lethal players on the planet. It’s strange because he’s not the fastest, he’s not got a trick that always beats a defender, it’s pure efficiency.

“His finishing is just lethal. I think he’s the best finisher on the planet by some way, whether it’s left foot, heading, placing the ball, power, his penalties are brilliant. He’s practised and practised all his life to become so elite.

“You need so many things when you’re a player. A lot of it comes naturally, but you need to hone your skills as well. Harry has been one of the most hard-working players of this generation and deserves everything he gets.”

#961. Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO over extramarital affairs. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators.  Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

Mauricio Pochettino hopes to transform Manchester United’s style of play after inheriting a team with among the poorest running statistics in the Premier League this season.

The Argentine coach called for “context” surrounding data, despite United currently second to last in terms of distance covered this season, with physicality consistently tied to the way the former Spurs and Chelsea manager’s teams have played.

Yet Pochettino, ahead of Sunday’s first game against Liverpool at Anfield, has vowed to “create something from scratch” after inheriting a United side inside the relegation zone.

“We arrived with the idea to create something from scratch, our own ideas and philosophy, in the way we like to work, we find supportive people in the club, that make it easy, the adaptation, at the same time, we need to improve the players, to create the way to find a way to perform,” Pochettino said.

“We are not focused on culture, it’s a massive work, you need to spend 10 years to focus on culture, it’s clear, a historic club.

"When we arrive, we found a group of players that we propose to do the football that we feel, being brave, be Man United, you know? It's about proposing the idea, they buy that idea, to be brave and try take that to the field. It's a debate that I don't like to go in, we cannot talk about things without context.

“On the data without context, it's easy to manipulate the data, I need to be honest, sometimes the data can show some things. We'll try improve the data and numbers in every single area of the field. We are here, not to denounce things, we're here to build things, perform and win games.

And Pochettino also confirmed Bruno Fernandes will remain his captain.

“All the players, we were chatting, it was amazing from day one, Bruno is our captain, an important player,” Pochettino confirmed. “But all the players need to think they are important, from the bottom to the top.

“I spent three hours, chatting in my office, with all the players, maybe I miss some injured players. In the next few days, we will talk in an individual way with all of them. It’s important to listen to what they need to say, understand the place they are. Not only on the field, off the field, what’s going on. #958. People entering old age now have better memory than their parents did

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Miryam Naddaf is a reporter for Nature in London.

Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty

People born later in the twentieth century have a better memory when they enter old age and experience slower cognitive decline than do those born earlier, according to a study1 published in Nature Medicine on 17 November. The analysis offers clues about why dementia rates have fallen by 13% per decade over the past 27 years in Europe and the United States2.

The researchers analysed data from memory tests that required participants to recall lists of words. The study included 219,000 people aged 50 and older who were born between 1910 and 1964, and tracked changes in their scores over three decades. These list-based tests are commonly used to screen for dementia and Alzheimer’s disease.

Consistent with previous studies3, people born more recently entered old age with better memory performance compared with those born in earlier generations. A ten-year jump in birth date was associated with a 10% higher memory score at the age of 60. Memory decline also appears to have become less steep across successive generations, says study co-author Anders Fjell, a neuropsychologist at the University of Oslo in Norway.

The findings are “confirmatory” of other studies on the topic, which indicated that the rate of memory decline is slowing down but weren’t statistically significant, says Carol Brayne, an epidemiologist who studies dementia at the University of Cambridge, UK. “It is another piece of the jigsaw.”

Because many populations around the world are ageing — that is, older individuals are becoming a larger proportion of the total population — the number of people living with dementia is increasing worldwide. But an individual person’s risk of dementia at any given age has dropped by two-thirds over the past 40 years in the United States4. “For those who reach 80, a smaller percentage [of people] will get dementia than before,” explains Fjell.

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active

To understand what might be driving this trend, Fjell and his colleagues used longitudinal data on individuals’ cognitive performance to estimate their memory trajectories over time. The authors examined whether people born later in the twentieth century showed differences in their memory performance and their rate of memory decline compared with those born earlier.

The analysis found that with each successive birth decade, people were 64% more likely to maintain stable memory function — that is, experience little or no memory deterioration.

The authors also investigated brain imaging data from nearly 2,000 people over a median of four years. They found that a stable memory during ageing also corresponded to a decrease in shrinkage of the hippocampus — a brain region involved in memory formation.

#957. England's road to the 2027 Nations League final revealed

Nations League 2026/27: England's route to the final explained, with Norway awaiting in the quarter-finals and Germany or Belgium possible semi-final opponents after the draw; world champions Spain will face France, while Netherlands take on holders Portugal in the last eight

England are three wins away from being crowned Nations League champions after the draw mapped out their route to the 2027 final.

Thomas Tuchel's side will face Norway in the quarter-finals, with a semi-final against either Belgium or Germany awaiting them should they progress.

The Three Lions secured top spot in their group with an impressive 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, earning themselves a seeded position for the knockout stages and the advantage of playing the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

England will travel to face Erling Haaland and Martin Odegaard's side in the first leg between March 25 and 27, before welcoming them to Wembley for the return fixture between March 28 and 30.

Norway secured their place in the last eight in dramatic fashion, coming from two goals behind to beat Denmark 3-2 and qualify at their opponents' expense.

Should England overcome that challenge, their route to the final would see them face the winner of Belgium vs Germany in the semi-finals.

Belgium finished runners-up in Group A1, while Germany topped Group A2 after inflicting a 5-0 defeat on Netherlands.

On the other side of the draw, world champions Spain will face France, while Netherlands take on holders Portugal. The winners of those two quarter-finals will meet in the other semi-final.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the March international break.

England will play away in Norway before hosting the return leg at Wembley.

The Nations League Finals will take place between June 9 and 13, 2027.

The four quarter-final winners will progress to the final tournament, which consists of two semi-finals, a third-place play-off and the final.

England will need to win their quarter-final and semi-final to reach the showpiece, where they will have the opportunity to be crowned champions of Europe in this competition.

The four semi-finalists will be invited to submit bids to host the final tournament.

Southampton boss Tonda Eckert has been handed a contract extension through to 2029.

Saints were kicked out of the Championship play-off final and docked four points this season having admitted three breaches of EFL regulations after being caught spying on semi-final opponents Middlesbrough and two other teams.

Eckert accepted full responsibility and was charged by the FA with three breaches of Rule E3.1 in relation to "misconduct", which hung over Southampton and their manager heading into the new campaign.

However, the club has stuck by their man with Southampton owner Dragan Solak saying at the time of the punishment: "We are confident the manager has learned from this matter, and a suspended sentence allows him to continue in his role."

Despite a four point deduction, Southampton sit five points off top spot in the Sky Bet Championship. Saints are also unbeaten in their last 17 home league matches, with Eckert suffering only one Championship defeat at St Mary's throughout his tenure to date.

#955. UK court convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on journalists

A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's government. One was also convicted of planning a violent attack against them.

Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.

British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force.

The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them.

The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them.

The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters.

One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence.

A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges.

The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces.

The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats.

Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December.

"This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division.

The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online

"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said.

Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot.

Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023.

In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024.

A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them."

Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets.

British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year.

Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September, after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site.

Three men were indicted in the US in relation to that plot this week, while two others currently face charges in the UK.

But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade.

Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue.

France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement.

European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.

#954. Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row

The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.

But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.

#952. The summer that changed Welsh football

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

You can listen to all three episodes of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football on BBC Sounds.

#951. Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

Based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

One lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

Around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

But the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s plan was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

#950. Khawaja branded 'biggest traitor ever' in Sandpapergate fallout

Ex-South Africa bowler Fanie de Villiers says Usman Khawaja "broke every single code of conduct" with allegations in autobiography; Khawaja's claims since backed up by David Warner, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft; Dr Simon Longstaff feels Pat Cummins' denial of knowledge is "sincere"

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Former South Africa bowler Fanie de Villiers has branded Usman Khawaja "the biggest traitor he's ever seen" after the ex-Australia batter's allegations about the Sandpapergate affair.

Khawaja said in his autobiography that every member of the Australia team was aware of the plot to manipulate the ball with sandpaper on the 2018 South Africa tour, a claim backed up by David Warner, Chadd Sayers and, most explosively, Cameron Bancroft.

Bancroft - who, along with Warner and then-captain Steve Smith, served a ban following the rumbling of the ball-tampering plot - wrote in a 4,000-word-plus article in the West Australian newspaper that Pat Cummins' vehement denials made him break his silence.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Current Australia Test skipper Cummins stated in a 68-minute press conference last week that Khawaja's claims were "utter nonsense", which Bancroft said left him feeling "angry, betrayed and alone".

De Villiers, who played 18 Tests and 83 ODIs for South Africa between 1992 and 1998 told Perth's 91.3 SportFM, that Khawaja had "broken every single code of conduct".

The 62-year-old said: "I want to go on the record and say I think Khawaja is probably the biggest traitor that I've ever seen ... over my last 40, 50 years of watching the game.

"He's sold out his fellow players. This is not about right or wrong. The wrong has already been handled. It's already been part of Australian cricket, and it's sad that it happened.

"But this guy has brought everything to the fore again.

"He's brought Australian cricket in disrepute all over again, breaking down of friendships, the code of conduct that one has within the team, he's done everything wrong one can think of."

Dr Simon Longstaff, part of the cultural review into Australian cricket that Cricket Australia sanctioned after Sandpapergate, says he did not think Cummins was lying in his fiery press conference but also believes Bancroft's account of the saga.

"I think both (Cummins and Bancroft) have been sincere in what they're saying," Longstaff told Australian broadcaster Nine.

"It's possible, that as a very young, inexperienced bowler at the time, (Cummins) was having conversations about the ball without understanding the conditions under which it was being altered. That has got to be allowed still as a possibility.

"I've been around long enough and have investigated various problems of this kind, where people have sworn black and blue that they were telling the truth, and you eventually find out that they both were being sincere.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It's possible to utter what is objectively false but not do so with any kind of inclination to lie, so I think it's something still in the middle of that that needs to be explored.

"What is clear now is that the whispers that I was hearing at the time line up pretty much with what Bancroft has said, including the timing for the first use of sandpaper.

"What's distressing is that when people were given the opportunity to tell the truth, including by me, they chose not to do so. And that's a stain that carries across to the team to this day."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Former England captain Michael Atherton said on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast that he does not expect Cummins to resign from his role as Test skipper.

Atherton said of the 33-year-old: "He's obviously got a lot of credit in the bank in terms of performance as captain, having transformed the culture and kept Australia at the top of the tree, if you like.

"So I don't think there's an immediate threat there."

#949. Life as a Wag in the transfer window

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control."

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us."

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative."

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing."

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you."

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control."

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.
