#891. Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics

Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

Against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

It was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

As in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

As much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he said, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”

The parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

The score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a big game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a new version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He said he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

“We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel said. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”

Ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, said England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

“We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”

Tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

“It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

“The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was important to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

“We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”

#890. Record crowds, legends - Bordeaux bid to escape amateur game

Bordeaux fans protested when the club were demoted to the sixth tier

The latest stop on Zinedine Zidane's homecoming tour was an important one for the new France head coach. When Les Bleus took on Turkey in Bordeaux on Sunday night, the ex-midfielder was returning to the city in which he spent four formative years of his playing career, between 1992 and 1996.

"I became a man in Bordeaux," Zidane fondly recalled in the build-up. France edged triumphed 2-1 with an uninspiring display, but it did not dampen the mood of the 40,000 fans inside the Stade Atlantique.

While the 1998 World Cup winner was not necessarily in familiar surroundings (the out-of-town stadium was built for Euro 2016, 20 years after his departure for Juventus), locals made every effort to make him feel at home, holding up a commemorative tifo before kick-off and chanting Zizou's name throughout.

Just a few miles up the road earlier that afternoon, Zidane's former club were playing their fifth match of the season in the sixth-tier Regional 1, in a north-western suburb of the city.

Thousands of Bordeaux fans had made the short away outing to Saint-Medard-en-Jalles' 3000-seater ground to watch their team seal a fifth win in five this season.

Girondins de Bordeaux, the six-time French champions, who were once regulars in European cups, now find themselves facing amateur opposition on a weekly basis.

Since 2022, the club has plummeted from Ligue 1 to the sixth tier through a combination of on-pitch struggles, mismanagement at all levels, and sanctions due to their financial troubles.

Listen to the latest Football Daily podcast

The club was taken over in 2021 by Gerard Lopez, who was previously in charge of Formula 1's Lotus as well as another French side, Lille.

While Bordeaux were already hamstrung by debts at that point, the situation on and off the pitch worsened under the Spanish-Luxembourgish businessman as the men's first team finished rock bottom of Ligue 1 in his first season.

A couple of seasons in Ligue 2 followed, before the club was docked down to the fourth tier in 2024. In their first National 2 season, they notably signed Andy Carroll but ultimately missed out on promotion.

The following campaign saw a repeat of that near miss, and the club was expelled from national-level football altogether this summer over their finances.

With Bordeaux left on the brink and whittled down to just eight full-time employees (down from around 250 a few years beforehand), Lopez sold up to Park Bench, a group of mainly British USA-based investors who also own Scottish side Dunfermline as well as a minority stake in Spanish second tier side Cordoba.

The supporters turned out in their numbers for the first home match of the campaign, which had been delayed amid the uncertainty over whether the club could continue running, against Stade Montois.

More than 11,000 tickets sold, a record crowd for that level of French football.

"140 years of history, we won't be stopped," read one of the banners held up by the Ultramarines fan group, who also made it a point to thank the seven first-team players who had stayed despite the club's double relegation.

The team is centred around a core of players with Ligue 1 and Ligue 2 experience. Steve Shamal, who scored a hat-trick in that 4-1 victory over Stade Montois, previously turned out for the likes of Caen and Annecy in the second tier.

"We know we should be higher up, but that certainty can also be a trap," said Shamal after the game. "We shouldn't think that it's going to be easy.

"We need to respect our opponents if we're going to put in good performances."

As the sixth tier of French football is regionalised, only the league winner in the Nouvelle Aquitaine region's top flight will earn promotion.

Their on-pitch success so far this season comes as little surprise given the gulf in quality compared to the rest of the league. Over the summer, Bordeaux notably managed to hold on to Europa League-winning full-back Almamy Toure, while former Belgian youth international striker Baptiste Guillaume also joined.

Several former players have also looked to get involved in Bordeaux's revival.

Benoit Tremoulinas, the former French international who was a part of the title-winning squad in 2008-09, notably announced that at the age of 40 he would be lacing up his boots again seven years after injury forced him to retire.

Paul Baysse, the former centre-back, is an assistant to head coach Arnaud Cormier.

Benoit Tremoulinas spent six years at Bordeaux, winning a league title and two cups, before also twice winning the Europa League with Sevilla

Perhaps the most significant endorsement the new owners could have hoped for was that of Alain Giresse, widely regarded as the club's greatest player. The Euro 1984 winner, who won three league titles while playing more than 500 times for the Marine et Blanc, was in attendance for the match against Stade Montois. He took the ceremonial kick-off before giving a full-time dressing room speech.

The new management unveiled their long-term plans for the club on Monday at Le Haillan, the city-owned training ground which includes a chateau that hosts the club's headquarters.

"We are humbled to have this responsibility," Park Bench investor Jeremy Green said.

"The club doesn't belong to Park Bench, it belongs to Bordeaux, it belongs to the 11,000 people who came to watch a Regional 1 game, to the players and to the community. We have a responsibility to rebuild this club.

"Our commitment to the community and to the players is that we will be fiscally responsible and patient.

"We're not a financial institution, we're a collection of individuals who bring with them business, sporting, analytical, and entrepreneurship skills."

Dominique Delport, the club's new president, revealed he knew Green and Twining through his wife, who studied at Oxford with them.

"We can learn from the club's golden years," the former journalist and advertising executive told BBC Sport, before adding that he would look to bring club legends to every league game.

Bordeaux won the Coupe de France as recently as 2013

While the club was sold for a symbolic euro, it did involve taking on long-standing debts which spanned transfer fees, stadium rent, and a compensation claim by former head coach Vladimir Petkovic.

Last Friday, the city's commercial court approved a request to restructure the debt as part of the club's continuation plan.

When Bordeaux were expelled from national-level football by the French FA at the start of the summer, the club used several avenues to appeal while the takeover was being finalised.

"We thought we had acquired the club in National 1 [the fourth tier]," Green and co-investor James Twining, told BBC Sport.

"Initially we walked away, but we were encouraged to come back," Green added. "We established that we were going to be able to restructure things and make it work.

"People around the club and in the local community encouraged us to try to find a way."

The six-time French champions have a long way to go before returning to the top flight.

"We're committing to a sensible financial structure, to a well-run club, and we're talking about 10 years to get this club back to Ligue 1," the new investors added.

A crucial step towards that long-term goal will be returning to the professional leagues, which would allow them to re-open the youth academy they were made to close when they dropped down.

Rebuilding the women's team, who were involved in the Champions League only a few seasons ago, is another one of the new owners' objectives.

Keeping the fans onside throughout the process will also be key, not least after the rift that opened up between groups during the previous ownership.

In any case, if the record-breaking turnout for Bordeaux's return to league action is anything to go by, their support seems unlikely to waver anytime soon.

#889. Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta

Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead

Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

By the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner. But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he said.

With Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage, that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is said to have admired from afar.

According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is said to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.

Nonetheless, Frank is said to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.

There is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.

For now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.

His Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish. Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.

The futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham.

The France striker tried to annul the final year of his contract after a move to Milan was scuppered by a failed medical in January and he is likely to push for a move again. But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.

#888. Joint-record six referee errors in last Premier League weekend

The failure to award a penalty to Arsenal would have been more controversial had the Gunners not scored a second-half winner

The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.

Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.

You have to go back to the early part of the 2023-24 season to find the last time there were six mistakes logged.

The statistic does not include correct VAR interventions to fix errors, such as the red card shown to Brentford's Igor Thiago.

In the last round of games almost every fixture had a contentious refereeing situation which was hotly debated.

It started on Friday with a potential penalty to Coventry City for a hair pull by Everton's James Tarkowski.

Arsenal were denied a penalty following a VAR review after it was deemed Kai Havertz was offside.

Tottenham lodged a complaint over a challenge by Leeds United's Jayden Bogle, who was not shown a red card.

And Liverpool argued against a late Crystal Palace penalty.

But which decisions did the KMI Panel rule were incorrect? Some of the votes might surprise you.

Such was the controversy across the weekend, it may come as a surprise that the KMI Panel ruled only two were missed VAR interventions. There have been six missed overall, the same number as this stage last season.

Incident 1: Coventry's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by Everton's James Tarkowski. No penalty was awarded.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi's hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened."

Incident 2: Arsenal's Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Hull City's Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Harvertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence."

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry

When the KMI Panel sits down to vote there are two separate considerations.

The first is on the decision of the referee, which is a basic judgement in law and the Premier League's expected interpretation.

The second is on the potential VAR intervention. This takes into account what the referee has said, the available replay angles and the high bar for intervention.

Incident 1: Thierno Barry put Everton in front against Coventry in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "On the balance of probability the ball did accidentally strike Barry's hand. However, the readily available footage did not provide conclusive evidence."

Incident 2: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty against Liverpool three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio. But was it just a clash of heads?

KMI Panel vote: 0:5 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "A penalty was incorrect with the contact being inevitable. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 3: Ipswich were awarded a 72nd-minute penalty against Bournemouth for a foul by Lewis Cook on Abdoul Ouattara.

KMI Panel vote: 1:4 incorrect on the field, but 4:1 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Ouattara made a clear step across Cook who didn't make a challenge and the referee's decision to award a penalty was incorrect. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 4: Potential second yellow card for Bournemouth's Marcus Tavernier.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field; no VAR intervention possible.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was a clear, deliberate action by Tavernier to delay the restart."

Some of the most high-profile decisions from across the weekend have not yet featured.

That is because they have been voted to be correct on the field and through VAR.

Incident 1: Leeds United's Jayden Bogle caught Tottenham's Mathys Tel on high on his ankle. There was no VAR review for a red card.

KMI Panel vote: 3:2 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "The majority felt Bogle was looking to challenge with his right leg and his left leg came down on the back of Tel's ankle without the speed, force or intensity to be serious foul play. Two panellists felt that the challenge was sufficiently dangerous to merit a red card."

Incident 2: Chelsea's Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge by Sunderland's Luke O'Nien.

KMI Panel vote: 4:1 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Clear contact made by O'Nien on Palmer which the panel felt should have been penalised with a free-kick on the basis that contact was made outside the area. One panellist felt that the foul contact was inside the area."

Incident 3: Sunderland were awarded a penalty when Levi Colwill was ruled to have tripped Brian Bobbey.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was upper body holding from both players as they progressed into the penalty area before a careless trip by the Chelsea defender."

Incident 4: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Lammens turned away from the ball, the contact he made on Suzuki was not impactful."

The KMI Panel was scrapped this summer in the Scottish Premiership because clubs became frustrated with the voting patterns of its members.

But it is more important in the Premier League, with the results creating a merit table which contributes to 50% of referees' salaries in bonus payments.

Many fans will feel there should have been more than two VAR errors logged in the last round of games.

Yet the KMI Panel does not exist to mirror the opinion of supporters.

Crucially, it uses the laws of the game and how the Premier League expects its games to be refereed as the barometer.

Still, six on-field mistakes - plus the Thiago red card - is clearly a high number.

And fans struggle to understand why it seems to be OK to have these on-field errors, and not correct them due to the high bar.

#887. Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’

Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them

In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”

With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, said, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they said, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, said he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

“We need time,” García had said. “We need to reflect.”

Instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho said before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

“Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

The games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season tour and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” said Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

In the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also announced they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he said.

Sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he said, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:

double quotation markWe have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing Even those who left us sing, from heaven This will never stop We will sing to eternity.”

Then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.

#886. Familiarity of Doha drives home just how far Socceroos have come in recent years | Joey Lynch

There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality, highlighted by a return to the scene of Asian Cup heartbreak

Last week’s 3-0 dismissal of Qatar at the Abdullah bin Khalifa Stadium marked the first time the Socceroos had returned to the Gulf state since their heartbreaking elimination from the Asian Cup just under three years ago. Back then, coach Graham Arnold called Doha a “home away from home” after they relocated there during the Covid pandemic, and went so far as to suggest that they would have some form of advantage at the 2022 World Cup as a result.

Wandering around the city in 2026, memories rush back of Socceroos fans becoming eager participants in the takeover of the city’s souks during the World Cup. So too the feelings of sadness to see the birds still cooped up in small cages at the nearby bird market. It evokes recollections of trips on the red Metro line out to the Al Janoub Stadium in Al Wakrah, aided by the faded posters and stickers celebrating the 2022 tournament’s arrival that to this day can still be seen in shopfronts. There’s the excitement, for some, when a stray cat reminds you just how personable the local felines can be, as well as the sense of unease that remains whenever one pauses to reflect on how all this was built and the hands that did so.

But for all the familiarity and continuity for the Socceroos – five players who were there when Son Heung-min broke Australian hearts featured in Friday’s win – being back in Doha rams home just how much has changed for this team, and how well and truly into a new era we are.

Tony Popovic occupies the dugout these days, after the defeat to Korea arguably represented the beginning of the end of Arnold’s tenure by sparking a fatigue that would culminate in a downturn in results and his resignation later that year.

Nestory Irankunda, the rapidly emerging star of Popovic’s team who now has eight international goals to his name, was about to suffer a 4-0 defeat against the Central Coast Mariners nearly three years ago. Alessandro Circati was left out of the Socceroos squad to ensure he retained his place in the Parma side seeking to secure promotion to Serie A. Paul Okon-Engstler, Patrick Beach and Lucas Herrington were all yet to play senior football.

These players, who all started against Qatar, are emerging cornerstones of a new Socceroos setup that fielded the World Cup’s youngest side in North America, before flashing signs of further growth against Brazil in September. On Friday, this talented group bullied the two-time defending Asian champions on their own turf in the first-half, putting the game to bed before Popovic swung the changes and things got disjointed after half-time.

There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality. Of players bringing to the national team the lessons they’ve learned not just in the green and gold, but also in their experiences at bigger, more demanding clubs and leagues – in part because of the platform they’ve been offered by Popovic.

All of which could make it serendipitous if Tuesday’s game against Jordan, at the symbolic home of his predecessor, proves to be the end of the Popovic era.

Sign up for expert analysis from Jonathan Wilson as well as a rundown of Australians playing in the major leagues

The players aren’t going anywhere but with his contract situation still up in the air, it could well prove to be Popovic’s last game in charge of the Socceroos if he doesn’t agree to an extension. Given the postponement of January’s Asian Cup, there may not be the send-off he might have envisioned. Instead, a 12,000-seat stadium – unlikely to be very full – will host a hastily relocated friendly that’s entire raison d’être has vanished.

Remarkably, after sensitive discussions to relocate Tuesday’s game after player resistance to travelling to Amman, in line with DFAT advice, Doha could once again be pressed into action to serve as a historic backdrop for the Socceroos, just as a pandemic already saw it become the site of many a moment of distinction.

#885. Eight-year ban for player who threw rock that hit assistant referee

The assistant referee had a 60-day recovery period after being operated on

An Ecuadorian footballer has been banned for eight years for throwing a rock at an assistant referee, leaving him requiring surgery to his face.

Jhon Perlaza was playing for Club Ciudad de Yantzaza against Club Rio Aguarico FC in a third-tier match in October when the incident took place.

The stone struck assistant referee Lenin Giovanni Ojeda Nunez in the face in the 96th minute of the game, which was subsequently abandoned.

A video on social media shows Perlaza standing up in the team's dugout to throw the stone, with Nunez instantly falling to the floor and holding his face after the object hits him. He then receives medical attention.

"The assistant referee suffered serious injuries that required surgery and a 60-day recovery period," the Ecuadorian Football Federation (FEF) said.

"The disciplinary committee found the player responsible for physical aggression against a match official and suspended him for eight years from all football-related activity, until 19 October, 2034.

"In addition, the FEF will ask Fifa to extend this sanction worldwide."

The FEF also fined his club Yantzaza $2,000 (Â£1,521) and ordered them to pay Nunez's medical fees of $4,369 (Â£3,323).

In a statement released on 20 October, three days after the match, Yantzaza apologised to the refereeing team and the fans, and confirmed Perlaza had been sacked as a result of the incident.

"As an institution, we categorically reject all acts of aggression, whether verbal or physical, both inside and outside sporting venues. We firmly believe that football should be a space of respect, coexistence, and fair play," they said.

"Once the person responsible for this regrettable incident was identified, the institution made the decision to remove him immediately, and he is therefore no longer part of our club."

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). Nature (2026) Cite this article

The Original Article was published on 24 June 2026

Retraction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10702-5 Published online 24 June 2026

The authors retract this article, following a suggestion from the editors. Shortly after publication, a preprint (subsequently published (see ref. 1 below)) by Till Sawala identified an inconsistency in our analysis. Our calculations were erroneously comparing the comoving distance between the observed galaxies to the luminosity distance between galaxies in the simulated mocks. Correcting these issues reduces the discrepancy between the observed and simulated samples to 1.48–2.75 sigma, depending on the sample construction. This falls below the standard significance threshold of 3 sigma in the cosmology literature.

Despite the revised uncertainties, our method remains valid and provides tentative evidence for anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of galaxies in the Universe. The revised paper, with corrected uncertainties, will be submitted to another journal. This retraction will contain a link to the new publication, if and when it is published.

#883. Five return for Wales' World Cup play-off final

Ceri Holland has not played for Liverpool since mid-September

Ceri Holland has been named in the Wales squad for next month's Women's World Cup play-off final against Norway despite being out since September through injury.

Olivia Clark, Hayley Ladd, Rhiannon Roberts and Ella Powell are also included after fitness issues, but Ffion Morgan, Laura Hughes and Scarlett Hill are among those who miss out with injuries.

The versatile Holland, arguably Wales' most influential player, has been out with a muscle problem, though she is thought to be close to returning to action for club side Liverpool.

Her involvement is a major boost for Wales as they attempt to reach the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Rhian Wilkinson's side face Norway at the Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday, 1 December, before the return leg in Oslo four days later.

Women's World Cup qualifying play-off final first leg

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Leicester goalkeeper Clark and Sunderland defender Roberts are also included even though they have not played since September, but the loss of promising Manchester United defender Hill is a blow given her impressive displays against Albania.

Crystal Palace's Ladd and Powell, of Bristol City, have played for their clubs since missing Wales' World Cup play-off semi-final games against the Albanians last month.

"For the play-off finals, just to have those experienced players back in the squad and on the pitch, I am very pleased," said Wales head coach Wilkinson.

"I think the blend of our young players and that experience is critical. The [young players] are almost naive, not understanding the play-off final pressure - it doesn't mean much to them. That's fantastic - that brings something to the group.

"Then we have the experienced heads who understand that the first leg is half-time, that a ranking is a ranking, that opposition hype is often merited, but equally they are just another team in our way."

With 204 caps between them, Hayley Ladd (left) and Rhiannon Roberts (right) bring welcome experience to Wales' squad

Winger Morgan had returned to action for West Ham after not being involved against Albania, but she is back on the sidelines after suffering a knee injury while playing for the Hammers last weekend.

Wilkinson said it is down to Morgan's club to reveal the extent of her injury.

"I haven't spoken directly to her, I've sent her a message," Wilkinson added.

"I think obviously when you pick up an injury and she's so proud of being Welsh and loves coming into camp... it's a double disappointment.

"But I'll speak to her later. Just give her some time."

Like Southampton midfielder Hughes, Mia Ross â who is without a club after leaving Charlton in September - is again missing from Wilkinson's squad, while Fulham full-back Charlie Estcourt is another absentee.

There is also no place for Sunderland defender Tara Bourne, who has switched allegiance from England to Wales, but is injured.

There is a recall for once-capped teenager Gwen Zimmerman, who plays for American side Northwestern NCAA, while Newcastle youngster Casi Gregson is included again after winning her first cap against Albania.

Wales start Nations League with home double-header

Wales in fight to retain rising female stars

Womenâs World Cup play-offs: How they work

Wolves midfielder Chloe Williams keeps her place having been a late call-up for the semi-final, while the only uncapped player in the squad is third-choice goalkeeper Soffia Kelly.

Wales are hoping to cause an upset as they bid to reach the Women's World Cup for the first time, though beating former champions Norway may not be enough to guarantee a place in Brazil next summer.

The complex nature of the qualification process means that Wales may have to negotiate inter-confederation play-offs next February to secure a World Cup place, even if they triumph over Norway.

#882. James Bowen latest jockey to reveal death threat incident

Bowen brothers were given security protection last year after a threat was made; fellow jockey Nico de Boinville revealed a similar incident earlier this week after threat made to Nicky Henderson's yard. Warning: Readers may find some of the language in this story distressing

James Bowen has become the latest jockey to reveal he has been subjected to death threats from disgruntled punters, with the 25-year-old disclosing that he and champion jockey brother Sean required security protection following an incident last year.

Nico de Boinville was in the news earlier this week when a threat against his life had been phoned in to Nicky Henderson's yard following the defeat of an odds-on favourite at Plumpton.

That was far from the first incident of its kind, and Bowen, speaking in his DragonSports blog while he recovers from a broken wrist, said both he and his brother regularly receive abuse on social media - but one incident in particular stood out.

He said: "Last season, at Ffos Las on October 16, 2025, we were both the subject of death threats during a race meeting, to the extent that we had security accompanying us between the paddock and weighing room for the next three or four days.

"It was something we kept largely to ourselves at the time, but recent events involving Nico de Boinville have brought the subject back into sharp focus.

"In our case, somebody made an anonymous telephone call, which I believe went to either the racecourse or the British Horseracing Authority, threatening to kill both me and Sean.

"It happened while we were both racing at Ffos Las. We were informed about it and, understandably, the authorities had to take it seriously.

"After our final race, we spoke to the police and explained everything we knew. There was security around us for the following few days, with people accompanying us to and from the paddock.

"Nothing much came of it afterwards, as far as I know, and we never heard anything further about who had made the call."

He went on: "You can perhaps understand why somebody might get frustrated if a horse they have backed gets beaten, but there is absolutely no justification for taking it to that sort of extreme.

"I hope the person who made the threat had no intention of carrying it out, but you cannot simply dismiss something like that.

"What is perhaps even more worrying is that receiving unpleasant messages has become such a regular occurrence that you almost become accustomed to it.

"I have had plenty of messages telling me they hope I break my legs or my neck. They tend to come through private messages on social media, particularly Instagram and X.

"It is not something that surprises me any more, which is probably quite sad when you think about it.

"You get hardened to a certain extent, and there is a bit of dark humour among jockeys about some of the things people send. Sometimes you have to laugh about it because otherwise you would cry."

If you have been affected by this story, support and guidance are available at sky.com/viewersupport

#881. The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry

Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?

Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.

Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.

Sunderland, wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.

But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.

Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.

In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.

That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.

Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.

This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.

The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.

This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.

Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.

Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.

While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.

Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.

Sunderland's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.

In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven â the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.

Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.

Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.

That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.

The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.

The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.

As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.

In that season, West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.

Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

#880. A long wait, some magic and that smile: Ronaldinho savours Ravenna debut at 46

Brazilian legend, an investor at Serie C club, showed glimpses of old brilliance as he played 45 minutes for the promotion-chasing side

It may have been the longest buildup in world football. In June, the former Barcelona and Brazil legend Ronaldinho was unveiled by the Serie C side Ravenna to make his comeback at the age of 46 – 11 years after his last official game. Then silence.

But on a chilly November day on the eastern coast of Italy, there he was, not only in the squad, but in the starting XI for the eagerly anticipated derby against Forlì as Ravenna chase promotion.

The Ravenna manager, Andrea Mandorlini, deployed Ronaldinho in a central position, just behind the striker Simone Rabbi. The Brazilian held his position well, but was slow to get going. As the game progressed, he warmed up and showed his excellent skills; some things do not appear to change. Ronaldinho touched the ball 25 times, took three corners – one of which nearly led to a Ravenna goal – and initiated the move that led to the hosts taking the lead in the 35th minute.

Having trained with the team just once, whether he plays again remains to be seen. But he had already sprinkled some magic on a club and a region that has not made headlines in years. He played the first half as Ravenna won 2-0 to stay second in the division’s Group B (the Italian third tier is divided into three regional sections). Only the group winners earn promotion and Ravenna trail Spezia by six points.

Whatever happens for the remainder of the season this has put the club back on the football map. Ravenna’s highest finish was eighth in Serie B, in 1996-97, but this match was broadcast live by Sky Sports in Italy and shown in several other countries. It even appeared on the giant screens in New York’s Times Square, where the club’s owners, the Cipriani family, have built much of their international reputation through Harry’s Bar.

The town’s mayor, Alessandro Barattoni, who, as always, was watching the game from the stands, said: “A champion like Ronaldinho, a world football icon, brings great visibility and today is an opportunity for us to showcase Ravenna around the world, from our stadium. It is something new for us and together with the club the municipality will try to understand how this can have a positive impact on the town.”

The local community had been excited at the prospect of Ronaldinho representing the club, but there was some regret, too. “It would have been nice if he had come to take a stroll around the city, among the people who live here and own the shops,” the barista Barbara said before the game.

So how did he end up here? The Brazilian is a friend of Ignazio Cipriani, the owner of the Giallorossi. Lorenzo Tonetti and Ariedo Braida, old acquaintances from Ronaldinho’s time at Milan, are also part of the club. They convinced him to become an investor in the club and to pull on his boots again. In addition, Ravenna are now wearing his R10 sportswear line and one of the stands bears the same name.

Ravenna are aiming high. Cipriani has never hidden the fact he is aiming for Serie A, which is ambitious for a city with a population of 156,000. And Sunday brought hope, Dinho stepping on to the pitch in a gold-trimmed kit picked by the club to celebrate his arrival (and available for sale at €120). His hair was kept in check by a black headband and he was wearing gloves on a chilly afternoon. On his back, the No 10, something more than just a number for him, the man who became a global hero thanks to his extraordinary skill and contagious smile.

A younger generation has been able to discover Ronaldinho’s genius through the endless supply of online videos showcasing his greatest moments. Children who have never seen him play know his tricks and signature moves, while their parents can relive an era of football they may feel no longer exists.

“Dad, was he strong?” a young girl asked her father as they walked hand in hand towards the stadium. “Yes, he was strong. Actually, he is strong,” he corrected himself.

Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in

One family had left Rome at 5am and travelled the 350km north just because their son had watched Ronaldinho on YouTube and wanted to see him live. Others had travelled even further, with supporters arriving from Turkey and Canada.

Ronaldinho hahas scored 299 professional goals, but his landmark 300th on his return was not to be. However, in front of a record attendance of 6,743 the way he initiated the move for Giulio Donati’s goal was ample reward for those who had turned up. Donati made his Serie A debut on 29 August 2010 for Lecce, at San Siro, against Milan, marking the Brazilian that day.

As Ronaldinho walked off at half-time, he was surrounded by a media scrum. After the game, he spoke of his desire to play again. “It all went by too quickly,” he said. “Football is like that, it’s always been like that for me.”

Who knows, perhaps he enjoyed himself so much that he wants to extend his career even further. “I don’t know, but if the president calls me, I’ll come back. It’s always a pleasure to play, I told him: ‘when he needs me, I’m there’.”

Mandorlini was effusive too. “We’re here and we’re truly proud to have been the architects of this match you played in,” he told the Brazilian. “So, if you want to play another one, that’s fine.”

Who knows what the future holds? For now, Ravenna fans will always have this: a day when a true legend connected people from around the world and allowed them, for one afternoon, to dream.

#879. Mauricio Pochettino’s USMNT time will be remembered fondly, but it wasn’t transformational

The incoming Manchester United manager improved the US team’s culture and competitiveness, but could not bring about sea change in two years

In a theater high up in a midtown Manhattan skyscraper built from lots of glass, a highlight reel played to deafening music. And then, on “a monumental day for US Soccer”, federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, announced they had bagged their man, Mauricio Pochettino, to become the highest-profile United States manager in the men’s national team’s history.

Pochettino held court for three-quarters of an hour in his signature blend of Spanglish before the assembled media and a grab bag of sponsors. Then he recorded some TV hits. And after that, in a bit of accidental prescience, he went off to record a podcast with Gary Neville.

Two years, two months, and a week later, he presided over the USMNT’s untroubled 2-0 win over Haiti in Cincinnati on Tuesday, putting a bow on an 8-0 aggregate victory in the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals. He did a lot of hugging afterwards, a staple of what was briefly mooted as Pochismo. He posed for a group picture with federation staffers. There were tears in the locker room.

After a 6-0 romp in the first leg on Saturday, Pochettino left his starting XI unchanged, raising some eyebrows. Perhaps he hoped to leave with another emphatic result; maybe he was buffing up his final stats in charge of the USA; or possibly he was legitimately concerned about giving away a lead of half a dozen goals.

It will probably be the last time in quite a long while that Pochettino enjoys a pair of consecutive lopsided victories. He boarded a private jet after the game to take over Manchester United just as soon it landed in England in the morning, leaving a situation where he enjoyed a bank vault’s worth of credit for one where his every result will be dissected and scrutinized for his viability in the job.

For all the hype, for the $6m annual salary – about double what the previous record earner at the federation, Jürgen Klinsmann, had made – and for all the talk of belief and culture and fight, what did Pochettino actually leave behind for his successor to build on? He was impactful, certainly, turning around a moody and slumping generation ambling into a home World Cup bereft of momentum or much discernible enthusiasm. The Argentinian roused the ballyhooed golden generation for four-fifths of a very strong World Cup, turning in displays more convincing and dominant than the program has ever managed on that stage – until it all came undone against Belgium in the last 16.

His time in charge was notable, absolutely. Pochettino got, and brought, lots of attention to the team, although it’s hard to say whether a more workaday manager might not have ridden that same World Cup wave, as the voice of the co-hosts.

Pochettino wasn’t the first USMNT manager to try to play more expansively, more technically, in a more aesthetically pleasing way. Klinsmann tried it, and Gregg Berhalter tried it, too. But Klinsmann didn’t have the players, and Berhalter’s weren’t ready for it. Pochettino did and they were, at long last, and he introduced a tactical sophistication, with deft attacking patterns that regularly unlocked useful spaces.

He also wasn’t the first USMNT manager to fixate on culture and give young talent a chance. But through his selections and his messaging, he reinstated an internal competition for playing time that had seeped away under several consecutive and at times complacent administrations. And he deepened the player pool considerably. Perhaps any old head coach would have spotted the glut of gifted teenagers pushing through and had the wherewithal to bring them along, but Pochettino deserves credit for leaning on the young players, handing them meaningful minutes and responsibility.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

While Pochettino leaves the USMNT better than he found them, his spell in charge was not transformational. He brought the Americans no further at a World Cup than they had been before. His statistics – victories in 62% of his matches; 2.08 goals scored per game; 1.29 conceded – are more or less in line with the numbers put up by his permanent predecessors. He did not win the Concacaf Gold Cup or the Nations League when he was occasioned to.

Nor did he take the US to their first World Cup in four decades, as Bob Gansler did in 1990. Or make them respectable on that stage, as Bora Milutinovic did in 1994. Or bring about their breakthrough, as Bruce Arena did in 2002. Or rebuild the program from its modern nadir, as Berhalter did in his first tenure. It is a sign of growth, perhaps, that the strides available to be made were smaller. You can only overcome the challenges you are faced with, after all.

Whatever the case, Pochettino will be remembered fondly by most. He smiled and joked a lot and did his best to say interesting things. He could be spiky, from time to time, but mostly injected an environment that had grown stale and dour with joy.

Pochettino, by all accounts, had a good time stateside, commuting here from his homes in London and Barcelona. He enjoyed watching NFL games and attended the Cincinnati Bengals’ home victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday. He got into country music, apparently. “Only we can say thank you,” Pochettino said in his final news conference, on behalf of his staff. “Thank you so much, and always we are going to keep the good memories.”

The USMNT, too, largely enjoyed their time with their famous coach. They made some nice memories together. But he may not have been here long enough to fundamentally change their trajectory.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

#878. Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time

Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.

European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.

French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.

Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.

Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.

In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."

McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

First, Fifa's executives backed Infantino at a crunch meeting in Rabat. Uefa then called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, while potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stay for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by Â£2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

With uncertainty over how much support Tashima will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.
