#861. Berrada on Carrick, Poch, defending club leadership and transfers

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada has spoken exclusively to Sky Sports about the start to the season; the United CEO discusses replacing Michael Carrick with Mauricio Pochettino, the futures of Bruno Fernandes and JJ Gabriel, transfer activity and the Man City charges

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

In a turbulent time at Manchester United, chief executive Omar Berrada has sat down exclusively with Sky Sports about United's start to the season, the decision to change head coach and facing fan criticism about the club's leadership.

With United in the relegation zone, the club sacked Michael Carrick during the November international break and replaced him with Mauricio Pochettino, who will take charge of his first game away at arch-rivals Liverpool, live on Sky Sports, this Sunday.

The change in head coach has followed a tumultuous opening few months of the campaign, with Lisandro Martinez also taking aim at the club's technical director Jason Wilcox for not preparing the team well enough in the transfer window, while Fernandes also criticised Carrick and his coaching staff's methods.

In this exclusive sit-down interview with Sky Sports' Patrick Davison, Berrada discusses:

Berrada believes United are going in the right direction, even though the club currently sit in the Premier League relegation zone ."One hundred per cent," he says.

"I know it's difficult to say this when you're sitting 18th in the Premier League table. It's clear - it's not good enough, not acceptable, and that's why we've made the change that we've made, so that we can move forward.

"But we are laying the foundations for sustained growth to put us in a position where we can be competitive consistently.

"The foundations are there. I am convinced that we are heading in the right direction."

Read below to see the best of the United chief executive's interview…

This is the third season in a row in which United have changed their head coach in the middle of the season.

This season strongly resembles the 2024-25 campaign that saw United decide to stick with Erik ten Hag despite the club speaking to other potential candidates - only to replace him with Ruben Amorim a few months into the new season.

As a result, the United leadership team has been questioned - even more so after United defender Martinez publicly criticised technical director Wilcox over the transfer window just gone.

Asked if it has been difficult to see the fan criticism about the hierarchy, Berrada says: "It is. I'm not going to lie. But let's be clear, we're not the protagonists. This is not about the individuals, this is about the club.

"This is about doing everything we can to make our fans happy, and that means improving the results on the pitch, and that means getting a team that is performing to its maximum potential, that the fans can feel proud of.

"Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and the scrutiny that we're going to get. We accept it, some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.

"I think we do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that."

There are lessons to be learned as well. "If you think about the fact that we've had three permanent managers in less than three seasons, clearly we haven't achieved the stability that we want to - that's for sure," Berrada adds.

"There are different circumstances as to why it didn't work out with Erik, Ruben and now Michael. And we're always learning. We're always trying to improve and understand what has failed."

However, while Berrada recognises the club's leadership hold responsibility for the club's success on and off the pitch, that responsibility also filters down to the players and coaches.

"It is our responsibility to run the club," he says. "And, yes, coaches have a very important role to play. Players, of course, have to perform at the highest level consistently for any coach.

"They're part of a club that when you're wearing the shirt, you have an enormous amount of responsibility. And that responsibility means that you have to be giving your best every day in training, in the matches. And that's the same for executives.

"So I understand the frustration from the fans. It's absolutely normal. My commitment is that we're going to do everything we can to make sure that we put ourselves in a position where we're competing to win titles consistently."

At the centre of United fan disgruntlement is the continued running of the club by the Glazer family, who work alongside INEOS chief Sir Jim Ratcliffe at the very top of the structure. Berrada insists, however, that the dual-running of the club is working.

"It's working very well," he says. "I know there's a lot of noise and people look for narratives in the media and that's fine, that comes with being part of this club.

"But from my perspective what I see is a very dedicated and engaged ownership group - both ownership groups. There's constant dialogue, we speak sometimes on a daily basis. Between them there's a very good alignment. I think they have complementary skill sets, if you want to put it that way.

"All the decisions that have been taken, we've been all on the same page, we're all supporting each other, and the shared ambition is to do what's right for the club."

So how did United come to the decision to remove Carrick? The former United midfielder was talk of the town at the end of last season after qualifying the club for the Champions League - but it all unravelled quickly after that.

Many felt United would remove Carrick after the 3-0 home loss to Bournemouth on October 25, but the club waited until the international break to make their move.

"It was a very difficult decision, to be honest, especially given all the affection everyone at the club has for Michael," says Berrada.

"When he took over the team last season, they did very well under him. They were playing some really good football, winning important matches. We qualified for the Champions League and finished third.

"We felt at the time he'd earned the right to continue leading the team. So when we started the season, it's clearly been a lot more difficult than we expected. The results haven't been good enough. I think we've dropped off in many areas.

"We wanted to give ourselves until the November international break to really take stock of what was happening with the team, what were the areas that needed to be improved. And in the end, we took the decision to make a change of coach.

"Unfortunately, sometimes when you're in the middle of the season, that's the one decision that you can make that can provoke a reaction, that can provoke a change in the dynamic. So that's why we had to take the decision."

The signs about Carrick's replacement, Pochettino, are very positive, according to Berrada.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Not only has the Argentine brought a degree of positivity to the club's training ground, but the United chief executive believes he has the "maturity" to take the Old Trafford reins.

"He has a tremendous amount of passion and energy," Berrada says of Pochettino. "We see it already in the two days he's been with us.

"There's a buzz about the place, and he's brought that with his staff. He has a very clear philosophy, identity of how he wants to see the team play. And I think he's coming just at the right time for him and us to be able to help the team and take us forward.

"He's equally as ambitious as we are, which is: we want to win titles.

"You have to think that when you're playing for Manchester United, when the results aren't going well, the pressure and the scrutiny is enormous. And all that noise around the club and around the players can be difficult to manage.

"So I think in Mauricio we bring somebody that has just the right amount of maturity and experience at the big clubs to be able to put his arms around the players and to let them perform at their highest potential."

"I think we've made progress in improving the squad over the last seasons." It is certainly a bold statement from Berrada.

United spent £163m on new players this summer - the majority of that on midfielders Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos.

With the jury still out on that trio, a lot has been made on the lack of activity in defence. Barring the introduction of Ayden Heaven from the academy, the United backline consists of the same players who were at the club five years ago.

As a result, United have one of the worst defences in Europe's top five leagues in terms of goals conceded.

But Berrada has defended the club's transfer policy - saying the previous summer's window where they signed Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha, Benjamin Sesko and Senne Lammens was a successful one.

"You have to take it in the context of the last few years," he says. "The summer of 2025, I think the recruitment team was widely praised with the four players that were signed. And they did very well. They helped the team achieve Champions League qualification.

"When we look at this summer, we went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play. It's probably been the summer or the transfer window where there's been the highest inflation in transfer fees.

"And we've said publicly and we've said consistently in the last few years that we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players for the right value at the right time in terms of what the squad needs.

"And when we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players that we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

"It's true that we lost Casemiro, who is a top player and gave a lot to the club. We also lost Manuel Ugarte to, unfortunately, an ACL injury. So our focus was very much about straightening the midfield.

"When we started the transfer window, we really only had Kobbie Mainoo as our midfielder. So we wanted to reinforce that, and we did it."

United were interested in defenders this summer, most notably Newcastle left-back Lewis Hall, but Berrada insists the club were not going to overspend on players in this inflated transfer market.

"When you look at the other areas of the pitch, and there's a lot of discussion about the back line," he says.

"But we did come into it thinking: we have depth. We have nine players that can play in the back line, in the back four positions.

"So that's why we looked primarily at investing in the midfield. But we were always looking for opportunities. I think it's been widely reported that we were looking at potentially the left-back position as a reinforcement.

"I think what we've seen in the back line is we've had injuries, it's taken Matthijs de Ligt longer than we would want it to get back. Unfortunately, Luke Shaw suffered a muscle injury that meant he was out for five or six weeks.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"So could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players and you have to find the right players at the right value.

"There's no point in us spending £40m, £50m for players that we're not convinced are going to add value to the team.

"So it's always about being disciplined and finding the right opportunities and getting the right players that are going to take us forward."

United also held interest in players such as Elliot Anderson, who moved to Manchester rivals City for £116m, and Berrada was pushed on the point about discipline in the transfer market.

"When I talk about being disciplined, I talk about not overspending on players that don't necessarily add quality to the team," he says.

"Because when you sign a player that doesn't work out for Man Utd, it becomes very difficult to move that player on or to get the sale we want. And that can set us back.

"So when I talk about being disciplined, I'm not talking about necessarily not spending to get the top players. We have the ambition to win, to win the Premier League, to win the Champions League, to win the domestic cups. And for that, we need top talent.

"So when we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don't want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

One of the main themes that could define Pochettino's time at United is the future of club captain Fernandes.

Sky Sports News has reported the Portuguese midfielder has turned down two new contract offers at the club, with his existing deal expiring at the end of this season.

There is a real risk the reigning Premier League and PFA Player of the Year could leave the club in the coming months.

"Listen, I've said before, we have a tremendous amount of respect for Bruno," Berrada says. "We're very fortunate to have him as a captain.

"What he's done for this team over the last six, seven years is absolutely incredible. Last year he won, I think, all the individual awards you can win.

"And we're very proud to have him as captain. It's true that we're having conversations about his new contract, but I prefer to keep that private. I think it's something that needs to be discussed behind the scenes between him and the club."

One player who is set to depart the club is 16-year-old talent JJ Gabriel - who announced his exit from the club this week amid an approach from Real Madrid.

United were not happy that Gabriel announced his departure without informing the club - and the entire saga has been a sour note on a club that has a long history of producing academy players.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"We did everything. Absolutely everything," says Berrada about Gabriel's situation.

"Let's not forget with JJ, he's a very young boy with a lot of media attention around him. Our primary concern is his well-being.

"Credit to the academy and people that have been here for many years, they helped him in his development. We still think this is the best place for him to continue his career and to grow.

"This club has a very rich history and tradition of developing young players and giving them the opportunity, as we're seeing this season with Shea Lacey. Obviously, Kobbie Mainoo has been doing well for us for a few years now - we're not afraid of giving young players opportunities.

"Obviously, him and his family have taken the decision to leave. We can only wish him the best.

"We want players that want to be here, that feel being at Manchester United is a privilege."

Berrada was also asked about his involvement in the Manchester City charges case.

In September, an independent commission found City guilty of breaching more than 100 of the Premier League's financial rules between 2009 and 2018. City are appealing against the ruling and deny any wrongdoing.

He was the chief football operations officer at City Football Group overseeing talent management, performance services and football intelligence between 2020 and 2024.

Prior to the role, Berrada had worked as chief operating officer at Man City from 2016.

"I'm not concerned," says Berrada when asked if there are any worries about his role at City.

"I want to be very clear about this: I wasn't involved in any wrongdoings. I wasn't involved in the proceedings. There are no allegations against me.

"In that sense, there will be no surprises."

But in another complication, Berrada could lead United in a compensation claim against his former club, should their appeal fail.

"I don't want to comment on that because right now, it's an ongoing process," he added.

"When it runs its course, then we'll take a view of what is our position as Manchester United."

#859. England fined for fans' anti-Catholic chants in Spain

The match between Spain and England took place at Atletico Madrid's Metropolitano stadium

England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.

European football's governing body have fined the Football Association Â£12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.

BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.

"We will not tolerate this unacceptable and deeply offensive chanting, and will work with the police, who attend all England home and away matches, to identify the perpetrators and take the necessary action," an FA spokesperson said.

A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.

Free Lions - the Football Supporters' Association Fans' Embassy for travelling England fans - says the team will be put at a disadvantage because of the actions of supporters in Spain.

"There is no place for offensive chants aimed at religious figures. The time for these chants is over," a statement read.

"The behaviour and reputation of England supporters abroad has improved significantly over the years but these chants undermine that progress.

"If the chants continue then thousands of travelling fans will miss out on future away games and players will miss that backing in the ground, putting our own team at a disadvantage, at one of the best times to be an England fan."

There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.

Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.

That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

#858. ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi

Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career

“I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds.

Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons.

“I’d get asked to go to a job or I’d even get booked for a job and they’d be like: ‘Oh, we want you to come to Germany for three days,’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to say: ‘I can’t do it, my priority is football.’ As fun and different as [modelling] is, it’s not my main job. Football was my priority and is my priority.

“It’s wicked, the stuff I’ve done modelling. Going to Milan fashion week, being taken to Paris fashion week with brands like Christian Louboutin is a level that I never thought I would reach or be possible when I first started it. Some of the people I’ve met doing it … when I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West … just celebrities and people that I grew up listening to and I feel like without that it probably wouldn’t have happened.”

Sowunmi takes the Nobu Pilates with teacher Marsha Lindsay class twice a month in the five-star hotel of the same name in central London. He is an imposing presence at 1.98m (6ft 6in) tall and grimaces through the session as his muscles are put to the test to keep him in shape for both his professions. It helps him to battle robust strikers and appear on social media as part of modelling campaigns. “Two days ago one of my current coaches said: ‘You popped up wearing a coat on my Instagram the other day. Can you get me one?’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to explain that it doesn’t really work like that.”

Sowunmi’s career path since he left his first club, Ipswich, without making an appearance has been that of a true lower-league player, taking in spells at Yeovil, Colchester and – between two stints with Bromley – Sutton. On the catwalk, he has rubbed shoulders with some of the biggest names in the industry while promoting designer brands and plans to continue doing that once he retires from the day job. He uses social media not only to post videos and images from photoshoots but to show the reality of life as a footballer.

“The fans and everyone that watches you on Saturday or Tuesday or whatever day you’re playing, they get to see you for 90 minutes and they don’t see the full dedication that goes into being a professional footballer,” Sowunmi says. “We’re away from our families for two days [for away games]; we’ll train on the Friday then leave, maybe have a seven-hour coach journey. We’ll have stuff to do at the hotel, stretching sessions, pool sessions, nutrition. We’ll wake up and we’ll have more stuff to do and it’s that whole buildup that I kind of want to show them and give them an insight into what we do.”

Last season Sowunmi helped Bromley gain promotion to third tier for the first time. The step up has been difficult, costing the long-serving manager Andy Woodman his job. “It’s been tough, as you can tell by the league position,” Sowunmi says. “It’s a completely different league. It’s taken a lot of the players by surprise, the difference between League One and League Two, but we’re grinding, we’re working hard and I’m sure it will turn for us.”

A carefully curated moustache sits atop Sowunmi’s lip to raise money for Movember. He is speaking at a charity event on Wednesday to highlight the importance of mental health, a subject close to his heart since his best friend took his own life. “It’s something that is really deep in my heart just being a voice for people and trying to help make a difference in any way that I can,” Sowunmi says. “I was actually on an away trip and I received a call from his dad to give me the news.

“Everyone was asking me what was wrong on the bus and that I wasn’t really speaking to anyone and then I think when we got home it was a four-, five-hour journey. The manager took me to the side and got me to open up to him a little bit. Looking back that actually helped a lot, so I thought if I can help someone to speak to someone or know that it’s fine to speak to someone then I’m definitely here for it.”

#857. New manager Frick to take Aberdeen back to basics

Frick has managed Vaduz and Luzern in the Swiss Super League

Aberdeen head coach Mario Frick says his track record proves he can produce exciting football - but for now a back-to-basics approach is required to save the Dons' season.

The 52-year-old arrived in the Granite City on a two-and-a-half year deal earlier this week to replace Stephen Robinson, who was sacked with the team second bottom of the Scottish Premiership.

Frick, who left Luzern in the summer after nearly five years in charge, has already identified a key problem he must solve quickly.

"I am known for high-scoring clubs. Twice with Vaduz we had the highest scoring record and last year with Lucerne, 76 goals," he said.

"I think Aberdeen is lacking goals [12 in 12 league games] so I am here to change that. On Thursday morning for the first time we did our attacking patterns and we have to improve now - we need time but we don't have it.

"More important now is to show the basics - body language, being willing to work, aggression, intensity - that is what I want to see on Saturday in Kilmarnock."

His first game in charge is a real baptism of fire for the Swiss-born former Liechtenstein player.

Defeat for the Dons would mean they replace their Ayrshire hosts at the bottom of the table.

The recent cycle of instability at Aberdeen is highlighted by the fact Frick - who was capped 125 times - has become their seventh permanent manager in six years.

But he is not daunted by recent history or by Aberdeen's situation - and sees similarities between the job he faces at Pittodrie and the one he inherited at Luzern in December 2021.

"I have had a very long career as a professional so I know the pressure. I am always an optimist and I know what I can do," he said.

"Luzern were at the bottom of the table with 18 matches and 11 points and the whole environment was sad and we saved them, so I am pretty sure we can do this also here.

"I am very ambitious. Now it is very important to get out of this situation but we want to go in the top six."

Hear from Aberdeen's Mario Frick at first press conference

Across almost three decades of working in the north-east of Scotland, I have seen many Aberdeen managers come - and go. In fact, far too many to name check.

From this side of the microphone, first impressions are always intriguing - and not always an accurate barometer for how things will play out.

For example, I watched Neil Warnock cut an impressive figure at his unveiling in February 2024 and look how that worked out.

So what are my early impressions of Mario Frick?

Well, having attended his maiden Pittodrie press conference, and observed him briefly at training this morning at Cormack Park - he exudes a calm authority.

He gives off the vibe of someone who knows where he wants to go, how he wants to get there and I suspect will probably not suffer fools gladly on his way to trying to achieving those ends.

Once both parties get to know each other a bit better, I also get the impression he will quickly command respect from the dressing room.

Frick appears to be a straight talker, and pretty clear in what he wants to get across.

While that obviously bodes well from a journalist's point of view, more importantly it could be crucial for the players as he looks to quickly deliver a winning formula that he, and the fans, hope can get the team moving back up the Premiership table over the coming months.

"With a manager change there is still a chance for every player to prove themselves, a new chance for everybody.

"To be honest I was really surprised with the first training session. It was brilliant and I saw a lot of quality.

"The facilities are paradise, it is incredible. It is better than in Switzerland so for me it is the next step. I am very happy to be here. I am very thankful to Adrian [Bevington, chief executive], Lutz [Pfannenstiel, sporting director], Mr Cormack [Dave, chairman], and the whole board."

"For eight years I have been a professional coach with only two clubs.

"Then I felt it is time for the next step. I waited for five months for this next step and when Lutz called me on Monday after the Hibs game I was excited from the first moment.

"I am really, really happy to be here because it is such a big club, such a famous club, a historic club, I am just proud to be here."

"Heavy metal, that is high-pressing, that is counter-pressing, vertical play, creating many goalscoring chances, that is heavy metal.

"In the next two weeks we have five games so I am just getting to know the new team and I have to make some very difficult decisions. But I am an optimist and I think we can do very well."

#856. How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

Impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers. Credit: Gandee Vasan/Getty

In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.

For Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect. Not only was he the sole bachelor’s programme student working alongside senior researchers with years of experience under their belts, he was also the only Black person in the lab. Although Asare’s mentor and colleagues were supportive and encouraging, he felt overwhelmed and out of his depth. “There was a steep learning curve,” he says.

At the time, Asare viewed his struggles as a sign that he didn’t belong in research. This feeling was compounded by the fact that he was surrounded by colleagues who didn’t share his background as a first-generation student from Ghana.

His experience, and those of many like him, is commonly labelled as impostor syndrome — the fear of not being as competent or knowledgeable as other people think, despite objective accomplishments. In a world that often prizes unflinching self-confidence and boldness, impostor syndrome is usually cast as a psychological flaw that the individual needs to ‘fix’. But it can be a natural response to working in a challenging environment or striving towards an ambitious goal, organizational psychologists say.

Impostor syndrome can also be a reaction to systemic bias and exclusion in the workplace, particularly for people from under-represented groups, including women, says Ruchika Malhotra, an inclusion strategist and founder of Candour, a workplace consultancy in Seattle, Washington. The company advises organizations on strategies to create diverse teams and inclusive cultures. One study1 conducted at universities in the United States found that women who work in scientific fields that particularly value intellectual brilliance are more likely to feel like impostors than are their male colleagues.

Much of the discussion about impostor syndrome pathologizes healthy self-doubt and shifts the responsibility onto individuals instead of the environments that exclude and marginalize them in the first place, adds Malhotra. “A lot of the ways that it’s been talked about haven’t been constructive,” she says.

Although it comes with drawbacks, in some situations, impostor syndrome can be beneficial. For instance, it can help people be better prepared and more focused, particularly when they have a long to-do list.

“Impostor thoughts are almost like your superpower when things get pretty overwhelming,” says Basima Tewfik, an organizational psychologist who studies impostor syndrome at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

Looking back, Asare says that his impostor syndrome prompted him to reflect on why he wanted to become a researcher in the first place. It has also made him more conscious of his resilience, how he needs to improve and when to seek help, as well as giving him more empathy. This has made him better able to support younger students and researchers who are feeling out of place. “It became my strength,” says Asare, who is now an oncology researcher and consultant at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, New Hampshire.

Impostor syndrome was first described as ‘impostor phenomenon’ in a 1978 paper on high-achieving women2 co-authored by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, both then at Georgia State University in Atlanta. They wrote that people who experience this phenomenon “maintain a strong belief that they are not intelligent; in fact they are convinced that they have fooled anyone who thinks otherwise”.

In the decades since, impostor phenomenon has morphed into a syndrome, even though it isn’t a medical diagnosis, nor is it classified as a psychiatric disorder. A review published in 20233 suggests that around 70% of people will feel unworthy of their accomplishments at some point in their lives. These feelings are even more prevalent in academia, with a 2012 study4 finding that as many as 82% of graduate students experience impostor syndrome to at least some degree. This pattern of thinking often affects high achievers and is associated with lower job satisfaction, hindered performance and burnout. Although some studies, including the 2012 paper, suggest that impostor syndrome affects mostly women and people from other groups under-represented in academia, others argue that it arises in specific situations rather than among particular groups. Relatively few studies have investigated whether commonly cited strategies, such as listing one’s accomplishments and accepting compliments from others, are actually effective.

Impostor syndrome has become a catchphrase in popular culture, with dozens of articles, books and courses describing what it is and how people can overcome it. But in the scientific literature, at least, the exact definition of impostor syndrome, or phenomenon, varies widely. This has created a murky picture of what it really is and how it affects people, says Tewfik. “There are a lot of different ways people describe this phenomenon,” she says. The loose definition has made it easy to confuse impostor syndrome, which causes people to make inferences about what other people think of them, with regular self-doubt, which is more of a personal reflection of your own capabilities, according to Tewfik.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers

Much of the research on impostor syndrome has also used measures that have made it difficult to distinguish from other psychological patterns, such as negative affectivity, a personality trait that is linked to a tendency to experience negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and insecurity, adds Tewfik. This crossover might explain why most studies on impostor syndrome have shown only negative outcomes, such as a lack of career planning and low motivation to lead5. “It’s possible that what we’ve been studying is actually something much more akin to fear,” says Tewfik.

This overly negative slant is exacerbated by the fact that many workplaces, including academic ones, place too much emphasis on self-confidence, says Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, an organizational psychologist at University College London. One 2024 study6 found that workers who display confidence are perceived as more competent and dominant, irrespective of their actual ability.

If impostor syndrome hinders a person’s ability to work or form relationships, it’s usually a symptom of a deeper issue or clinical condition, such as an anxiety disorder. But feeling like you’re about to be ‘found out’ before delivering a big presentation, for example, is usually a sign that you’re being challenged or working outside your comfort zone, says Chamorro-Premuzic. “There is a very healthy degree somewhere that we’re not appreciating,” he adds (see ‘A toolkit for working with impostor syndrome’).

In scientists, impostor thoughts can simply be a by-product of thinking critically and approaching things with a healthy dose of scepticism, says Samantha Sutton, an independent career coach for scientists in Boston, Massachusetts. It’s also often a natural response to working in a high-achieving, competitive environment or towards an ambitious goal and should be normalized instead of treated as a problem to solve, she adds. “If you’re up against something big, you should be scared,” says Sutton. When she communicates this to her clients, they are often relieved to hear that they don’t need to strive for total self-confidence before taking steps towards their goals. “They realize that nothing is wrong,” adds Sutton.

#855. Miami Magic fancied for Newbury gold as ante-post selections revealed

With the National Hunt season clicking into gear, the Weekend Winners team nominate their ante-post fancies for the coming months; watch the episode in full on the At The Races YouTube channel

On the latest episode of Weekend Winners, the panel reveal their top ante-post bets for the upcoming winter months.

Host Kate Tracey looks to next week's Coral Gold Cup at Newbury for her selection, with panellists Declan Rix and Sam Boswell setting their sights on races on the horizon.

"I like an old favourite of the show who has returned in good order this season in King Turgeon for the Becher Chase. He is in both the Grand Sefton and the Becher, but he must run in the Becher. He is such a good jumper, and he has won a Grand Sefton before.

"He is a horse that is so, so progressive and last season was a disaster. He has had a wind operation, and he looked like he took a blow at Aintree. We saw signs of life in the stable of David Pipe; he will be for me at a good price."

"I'm aiming for the Coral Gold Cup next week and I like Miami Magic for that. His chasing debuts weren't anything special when getting beat at short prices but he got his act together later on in the season.

"He ran well over hurdles in a Pertemps qualifier last month which gave him a perfect prep. He is a second-season chaser, which means he fits the perfect profile for the race and he's a good price for this race. Hopefully he can go well."

"With plenty of the possible King George VI field not looking likely to turn up, it's more and more obvious to just back Kitzbuhel for the race on Boxing Day. He's Kempton proven, the ground he is proven on - I think the race will decimate and I think he is the one that we will see this weekend for a prep and then kick on to here."

#854. Struggling Blackpool sack Evatt on his birthday

Ian Evatt won 23 of his 57 games in charge of Blackpool

Blackpool have sacked head coach Ian Evatt on his 45th birthday after a year in charge following a run of one win and six defeats in their past 10 league games.

Evatt's final match was Saturday's 1-0 away defeat by fellow strugglers AFC Wimbledon, leaving the Tangerines immediately above the League One relegation zone.

That defeat, however, came after the he said his squad had been decimated by a sickness bug during their trip to the capital.

Evatt departs the Seasiders with the announcement made a matter of hours after the club wished him a happy birthday, external on social media.

In a statement, the club thanked Evatt for his efforts and said Steve Thompson will take charge for Saturday's game against Wigan Athletic.

Blackpool announced Ian Evatt's dismissal less than seven hours after wishing him a happy birthday

Blackpool appointed Evatt, who won promotion from League One and the Championship during seven years as a centre-back for the club, as Steve Bruce's successor in October 2025.

During a six-year playing career at Bloomfield Road, Evatt made more than 250 appearances for the Seasiders.

On arrival as a manager, a tally of 13 points from a possible 15 in December 2025 lifted them out of the relegation zone, although they lost 10 and won two of their next 15 matches in all competitions.

They finished the campaign strongly, with six wins in seven games as part of a sequence of one defeat in 13 between mid-March and the end of August, only to struggle again as this season continued.

Speaking after their defeat by Mansfield in October, Evatt said he had "a huge amount of confidence" in his ability because of his record.

Evatt guided Barrow to the 2019-20 National League title in his first managerial role, then won promotion to League One with Bolton Wanderers the following season.

Wanderers went on to lift the 2022-23 EFL Trophy and reached the third-tier play-offs in consecutive seasons under Evatt, losing in the final in his final full campaign in 2023-24.

'It's been horrific' - Evatt says sickness bug decimated Blackpool

BBC Radio Lancashire sport editor Andy Bayes

After an encouraging start to the season, Blackpool's form has been alarming since the beginning of September, and owner-chairman Simon Sadler has decided a change was needed with 33 league matches still to play.

There have been mitigating circumstances but everyone in the hot seat is judged on their points return.

His final game in charge will undoubtedly go down as one of those factors. Illness within the squad made the defeat at Wimbledon somewhat understandable, but the performance should have warranted more.

Throughout Evatt's tenure, he was forced to constantly juggle an injury list that never seemed to ease.

The centre-back position was a recurring problem and is unlikely to be solved overnight. Steve Bruce signings Fraser Horsfall and Michael Ihiekwe have yet to make a league appearance this season, despite being expected to play a significant role after injuries at the back end of the last campaign.

Supporters wanted greater tactical flexibility and a system that would allow mercurial talents such as Josh Bowler to have a greater impact.

However, Evatt largely stuck with a wing-back formation, believing he did not have the personnel to play effectively in other ways.

He made an immediate impact after taking charge, but that was followed by a significant downturn in form before a recovery that secured League One survival last season.

This term, there had been hope that those struggles were behind Blackpool.

Evatt will retain legendary status for his achievements as a player, having won two promotions and played in the Premier League.

However, Blackpool are now searching for their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Sadler took over the club in the summer of 2019.

#853. The best European strikers this century - ranked by you

The top 10 European strikers of the 21st century

Classic number nines, penalty-box poachers, troublesome targetmen and tireless all-rounders.

There is no one-size fits all when it comes to determining great strikers, but they do all share a common trait - a ruthlessness in front of goal.

This week, however, we put the power in your hands to decide the best European frontmen of the 21st century.

Tens of thousands of you voted on the 20-man shortlist drawn up by our panel.

We then asked European football experts Guillem Balague, Julien Laurens and Raphael Honigstein to discuss your choices on the Euro Leagues podcast.

So from 10-1, here are the best European strikers this century - as voted for by you.

Top 10 European Strikers of the Century - Part One

Karim Benzema comes in at number 10, the former Lyon and Real Madrid frontman's closest challengers coming from across the continent in the shape of Raul, Robin van Persie, Michael Owen and Miroslav Klose.

Laurens: "From a young age you could see he was something special. I know it was difficult at the beginning at Real Madrid, but in the post-Cristiano era he carried that team, wore the armband and won big titles and trophies by being decisive in big moments. Like I used to say 'Karim the dream'."

Honigstein: "The selflessness, the ability to work for the team. A sense of elegance and humility on the pitch, which is unusual in a goalscorer. I think he is unusual in that list. I think not many will define themselves through their teamwork and assists as much as their goals, but he was that player."

Ruud van Nistelrooy edges Benzema, with whom he briefly overlapped at Real Madrid - the Dutchman teed up the Frenchman and scored himself in their only La Liga appearance together, before he left for Hamburg in January 2010 following injury problems.

The former PSV striker's most consistent spell, of course, came at Manchester United, where he scored 150 goals.

Honigstein: "He is the nicest guy but he never came across that way on the pitch. Typical trait of a striker, he would kill to score the goal. I think anyone who has grown up with him scoring goals, for United especially, must have a soft spot for him because he was a phenomenal poacher."

Laurens: "He was a strong player physically, and despite the lack of pace the awareness in the box was just very special even with all the injuries."

Zlatan Ibrahimovic slots in at eight, comfortably clear of Van Nistelrooy and Benzema. The Swede netted more than 500 times in a career that spanned Malmo, Ajax, Juventus, both Milans, Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Manchester United and LA Galaxy.

Balague: "He was a big-game player and that explains the league titles with PSG. Scoring four goals against England, the overhead kick. The personality thing has put him one or two places in this list, saying 'I am great, I am the best'. If you keep saying you're great it makes people stop and think."

Laurens: "The mentality of really believing he was the best and nobody was better than him, apart from maybe Brazilian Ronaldo, who was his idol growing up, and he would watch videos of him and try to replicate in his council estate. If you watch a highlight reel of his best goals he was incredible."

Honigstein: "What makes him unique among the strikers is his technique, You could see elements of martial arts in his goals. No-one scores goals like that."

The first Englishman on the list, although the third to have represented Manchester United - it's the Old Trafford outfit's record goalscorer, Wayne Rooney.

Honigstein: "I don't think there is anyone who would've watched English football at that time [early in his career] and not been enthralled by his game. The only downside is the combination of injuries and not the most professional lifestyle meant he did not fulfil his potential. He could've been Messi."

Balague: "What could have been, yes. He was the national team's record scorer too before Harry Kane took it. I find him to deserve this place as he had to adapt to a lot of strikers and he did it well. He had the ability to link up and score. He was very intelligent."

Laurens: "He is the most street footballer England has ever seen. There's no rules, that kind of anger you saw on the pitch. I don't think people in England realise how good he was."

What does becoming the all-time World Cup top goalscorer get you? Sixth place on the best European strikers this century list. The Real Madrid forward, 27, just misses out on the top five.

Laurens: "Maybe if we do this ranking again in a few years he will be higher. I would have had him top five, for sure. He has scored more than 400 goals. I don't think Messi and Ronaldo had scored that many at that age, so he's ahead. I don't know if he will play for as long as them but he hasn't done much wrong in his career."

Balague: "This list has to do what you feel about the player, not science - 22 goals in 22 appearances in World Cups and [Euro] Championships. He should be at least top three because of that. Great stats, but we're not in love with him."

Honigstein: "I don't think there is a forward that is as good as footballer as him in 2026. On that basis alone he should be higher, but people when they vote have other things in their head. The only way to win everyone over is to score more goals and win more World Cups for France, which I think is possible."

There was little between Mbappe and Erling Haaland, but it is Manchester City's prolific Norwegian who slips in at fifth. The 26-year-old has already scored more than 300 club goals and has a staggering 68 in 61 games for his country.

Balague: "Mbappe should be higher than him. Haaland scored 52 goals in 53 games [in 2022-23], that is astonishing, but he's gone 11 finals without scoring. We're talking about the best. We're talking about what we see at the moment and what we see is someone who is calculated but in a more charming way. An ability to score we haven't seen in a while; power, ability to finish. He is not world class to the level of others."

Honigstein: "I don't think it's fair to judge him on just that. They [Manchester City] won the Champions League when he was there. When Haaland arrived with Pep Guardiola, they found a way to do it. What makes him unique is the physical attributes and the pace. To have both is unique. He can sprint like a 100m sprinter. Is he the fifth best striker of the 21st Century? I don't think he's that far behind."

Interesting, this, because Robert Lewandowski is well clear of Haaland in fourth, but the leap from the Polish forward to the top three is massive - more than 10,000 votes.

The 38-year-old is still chipping away for Chicago Fire in Major League Soccer, having been a reliably ruthless assassin for Barcelona, Bayern and Dortmund.

Honigstein: "He used to play basketball, judo, handball - his father wanted him to have a wholesome education. You could see his completeness that he had as a centre-forward. Nothing in his game was extraordinary but in terms of ticking all the boxes, none come close to him."

Balague: "He said he learned to be an elite striker when he forgot what he had just done, like a fish. Mistakes he had in his head affected his performance. One day he just continued like it didn't matter."

Laurens: "He won the Ballon d'Or in Covid, it won't be on his mantlepiece but we all know it was his."

Fresh from his Ballon d'Or triumph, England's record goalscorer and appearance maker rides into the top three on the back of 61 goals in 51 outings for Bayern Munich last season.

Kane left the Premier League three years ago with the second-most goals ever in the competition, and is also Tottenham's all-time record scorer.

Honigstein: "Third place, at least. He is doing incredible things. At 33, still not quite at his peak. I don't think he relies on his pace, physicality, it's all about intelligence, technique. I don't think there's anyone in the game that strikes a ball as well as him right now. I don't think any player comes close that we've talked about so far in overall work-rate, defending, helping the team, making tackles in your box in the 90th minute when you're 3-0 up because he's that kind of guy. He is humble and a superb human being."

Laurens: "What I love about Kane, from a young age, a lot of this list you just knew the trajectory would be all the way to the top. Kane was not like that. It could have been very different for him. Nobody at 17 would've said he was going to win the Ballon d'Or. Nobody believed in him like the others. Kane had a very different journey."

Runner-up Thierry Henry is the only striker in the top six who is retired. A World Cup and Euros winner with France, Henry won titles with Arsenal - where he scored 228 goals - and a Champions League with Barcelona.

Honigstein: "During his time, I don't think there was a player like him in the Premier League. The way he played football was stylish, elegant, but there was almost a kind of a romantic connection between him and the ball. I don't think there was anyone near that kind of level of technique and, for want of a better word, va-va-voom he exuded. That just made for amazing viewing."

Laurens: "For me as a fellow Parisien, he's a very special player, a very special man. A career that has been incredible from a young age. It's that season in the Premier League - 24 goals, 20 assists in 38 games - not even Kane or Benzema or Cristiano, OK, Messi is different, but they haven't done that and yet he did it.

"There are still some people who undervalue him and underappreciate him and the monster that he was on the football pitch. He had it all. The pace, the style, the elegance, the technique, the mentality, the goals, the aura, the charisma. Just everything you wanted if you were to build a striker. One of the greatest football brains ever."

Of course, at number one, it's the man chasing the 1,000-goal dream. Cristiano Ronaldo may have retired from Portugal duty with 146 notches on his strike chart but the quest goes on at Al-Nassr.

The 41-year-old's evolution from tricky winger to prolific frontman has taken him from Sporting to Manchester United, twice, Real Madrid, Juventus and now Saudi Arabia.

Balague: "He's the best striker in history. His numbers are incredible. He won't stop until he gets to 1,000. He is somebody who is special. We know his background, how he wanted to be Ballon d'Or winner at 12 and didn't stop until he got there. He ran up the mountains of Funchal with weights in his ankles and snuck into the gym when it was closed to get the physique he wanted."

Laurens: "Always in the right place at the right time. The instinct. He was born with a gift, like all in this list. But you still have to work hard. Nobody will ever reach those levels again. 1,000 goals for club and country will never be done again, I think."

Honigstein: "Peak Ronaldo for me was Gareth Bale scoring and him looking very unhappy. I don't think there will be any dispute about him being the greatest. Somebody who has done it all, won it all, and he's still going for the love of it."

#852. Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’

A 14-year civil war ravaged the country and ground women’s football to a halt. Today, the first glimmers of hope are beginning to emerge amid difficulty

In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close.

Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home.

Scared, exhausted and running on adrenaline, the team had lived through another episode of disruption; but in truth they had rarely known stability. For Syrian women’s footballers, navigating uncertainty had been part of the game long before the country’s political upheaval reached its latest turning point. “My generation was burned away and completely lost,” said Noor Jumaa, a former national team goalkeeper. “It was like everything that was being built just disappeared.”

After 14 years of war, Syria has much to rebuild. Women’s football is among the institutions trying to recover from a conflict that erased an entire generation of players, interrupted the development of the game itself and left its infrastructure struggling. Yet, in recent years, Syria’s youth teams have emerged as one of the country’s more unexpected sporting success stories, winning regional titles and producing players who are beginning to make their mark abroad.

Syria’s women’s national team played their first international match in 2005. By 2011, plans were under way for an 11-a-side women’s league. Then the uprising began, and all plans were abandoned. For the next six years, women’s football in Syria effectively stopped. There were no international fixtures at any level, only occasional futsal tournaments. More than six million people eventually fled Syria, including hundreds involved in the sport, leaving an already small pool of players scattered across the world.

Men’s football, by contrast, continued. The national team played matches abroad after Syria was barred from hosting fixtures in 2011 on security grounds. The Assad regime used its successes to project an image of normality, even welcoming the squad to his palace after their 2012 WAFF Championship victory. Fifa, despite its rules against political interference, stayed silent.

Girls growing up in those years had no women’s team to watch. “I was watching a match of Syria’s men’s national team, and I was really upset. I would say, ‘God, if only they’d make a national team for girls,’” recalled Raneem Abo Lateef, a 21-year-old goalkeeper for Syria. The opportunity came unexpectedly after her family moved houses, and a girl next door told Abo Lateef that a relative was starting a girls’ club. “Girls’ football? Wow,” she said. “It was like dreams coming true.”

Similarly, international teammate Julnar Mustafa spent hours playing with boys in her neighbourhood in Hasakah. Born in 2008, so too young to remember the beginning of the uprising, she filmed herself dribbling and performing tricks on her phone, uploading the videos to Facebook. A regional coach came across them and invited Mustafa to join his team.

But finding an opportunity to play was only part of the challenge. “In our society, especially in the north, in Hasakah, sport is completely off-limits for girls,” Mustafa told the Guardian. “Not football, not anything”.

While a new generation of girls were finding their way into football, the national team was attempting to return to international competition. In April 2017, Syria entered the Asian Cup qualifiers in Vietnam, assembling a squad after six years without any activity. The federation announced tryouts on Facebook, and players were given about a month of preparation. Syria went on to lose every match, including a 14-0 defeat by Myanmar. “Honestly, it was one of the worst teams in Syria’s history,” said Jumaa, who was part of that squad. “We lost by terrifying scores.”

Maha Al-Katreb, also in the squad at the time, remembers the criticism that followed. Players were ridiculed despite having had little preparation. At the tournament, she saw opponents arrive with larger coaching staffs and younger players training alongside their senior teams. The gap between Syria and their regional competitors was difficult to ignore.

With injuries ending her career early, Al-Katreb fell into coaching by chance and turned towards building a programme that could develop the next generation. She later joined the Syrian Football Association (SFA), taking on administrative and coaching responsibilities.

A six-team women’s senior league was established in 2019, followed by the development of youth national teams. This year the country held an inaugural edition of its youth league. Al-Katreb developed Syria’s first women’s football strategy, submitted to Fifa, that set out a longer-term plan for expanding participation and creating a pathway into the national teams. “You have to start building from the bottom if you want to see results after these 10 years,” Al-Katreb said. “So that we don’t burn one generation after another.”

In 2022, women accounted for only 1,000 of Syria’s 25,000 registered footballers. The women’s football strategy, seen by the Guardian, aimed to increase female participation by 150% over four years, including through 33 school training centres across 11 provinces, with capacity for 1,650 girls by 2026.

The government has also outlined plans to rehabilitate the country’s sporting infrastructure. Rami Alsubea, an adviser at the Ministry of Sport and Youth, said in a statement that 48 sports facilities had been rehabilitated in 2025, with plans to rehabilitate about 150 more and build about 20 new ones by 2028. Restoring infrastructure is in part to meet hosting criteria set by Fifa and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

Al-Katreb left the federation more than a year ago. Jumaa is now part of a two-woman team leading its women’s football department, appointed after the arrival of the federation’s current president, Feras al-Teet. Several players have criticized the federation’s leadership and the pace of progress. The Guardian reached out to Al-Teet for comment. He declined.

Among the players who have been vocal about the shortcomings is 26-year-old Rona Aizouk, one of the most experienced members of the current generation. Named after Brazilian footballer Ronaldinho, she made history in 2023 when she became the first Syrian-born woman to sign a professional contract, joining Saudi side Najmat Jeddah. Her performances in Syria had attracted the club’s attention, but securing the move proved difficult. Visa refusals and paperwork complications delayed her arrival until two days before the season began. Her time in Saudi Arabia lasted only a few months, and she was unable to extend her stay.

“Honestly, I went there not wanting to come back,” said Aizouk. “There’s no comparison. Everything is better, the treatment, the training, the facilities. It’s just different.

“The most important thing is the players’ comfort. Here in Syria, we have to endure psychological pressure and torment. As a player, I have to fight the world just to achieve even a little bit of success.”

After returning to Damascus to complete her studies, Aizouk quickly received interest from multiple clubs in Jordan, where she now plays. For her, being in situ abroad is about more than personal progression. “I want to be a message that I, who came out of hard circumstances and out of a war, still managed to succeed.”

Aizouk’s exposure to regional excellence has shown her that Syria is still many years behind. At the forefront is financial restriction that has left the sport bare-boned. International sanctions and banking restrictions imposed on Syria left millions of dollars in development funding from Fifa inaccessible to the SFA, preventing it from fully benefiting from programmes such as Fifa Forward.

Although broad economic sanctions have since been lifted, an estimated $11.5m in funds remains inaccessible to the federation. Both the SFA and Fifa insist they are working to establish a mechanism through which the money can be transferred. For now, the support has been seen in training equipment.

The financial strain is felt directly by players as both the national team and regional league are operated by the SFA. Clubs frequently go months without paying wages, and when payments do arrive, players say they can fall short of the amounts agreed. International call-ups offer little relief: during national team duty, including training camps, players receive a daily allowance of $20, capped at $200 for the length of their stay, regardless of how long it is. Some say the costs of travelling and playing can exceed what they receive.

Several clubs have folded since the domestic league’s launch in 2019, citing financial difficulties and the continued disruption caused by the war and ongoing conflicts. Those that remain often struggle to provide even basic resources.

Al-Hilal, now renamed Qamishlo Sport, have become one of the country’s most successful women’s sides, currently reigning as senior and youth league champions. But their achievements have not translated into financial security, according to head coach, Daleel Khalid. “There’s an absence of adequate support from all sides and the parties responsible for Syrian women’s sports, whether in terms of training camps and preparation, or the capabilities and infrastructure needed to develop the game,” he said.

The club’s campaign at the 2026 WAFF Women’s Clubs Championship was a big test. The tournament brought together league champions from six regional competitions. Despite having only a short training camp at home, Al-Hilal reached the final against Saudi champions Al-Nassr. Abo Lateef and Mustafa were among those who represented them, and their performances offered a reminder that Syrian teams can compete with the region’s best, even when their opponents have considerably greater resources.

There was also individual recognition. Al-Hilal’s Mai Al-Jani was named the tournament’s best player after a series of standout performances, an achievement she was quick to share with those around her. “The award I won is a source of pride for me, for the club and for the players. I see it as a team award,” she said. “It belongs to the staff, the players, and every Syrian girl living through these difficult circumstances.”

Born in 2006 in a small village in Homs province, Al-Jani has emerged as one of Syria’s promising attacking talents. She won the league’s Golden Boot in the 2024-25 season and has continued to impress for both club and country. She was also named the best player at the 2023 WAFF under-17 championship, when Syria won their first international title in women’s football. Al-Katreb, who was an assistant coach, saw the victory as evidence of what the country could build with the right support.

The WAFF under-17 triumph was repeated at the 2026 edition with a completely different squad. “It was joy that everyone in the country needed,” said Jumaa. “We were completely outnumbered in technical and admin staff, with only nine of us managing everything. Other teams had double the number of staff, with gameplay technology we can’t get our hands on.”

For Abo Lateef, the greatest risk is allowing another generation of players to lose the chance to compete. The senior women’s national team, for instance, has not played in over two years, with no reason given to players. “We need competition, regardless of the level,” said Abo Lateef. “I’m afraid a day will come when I’m made to sit at home, as was the case with the ones before us. A friendly fixture is a good start. Anything.”

Aizouk’s message to those responsible for the future of the women’s game was more direct. “Save Syrian football,” she said. “Save the generations. Save us.”

#851. Czechia braces for massive protest against public media reform plans

A fast-tracked bill to cut public media funding has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is planned for Prague on Sunday.

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.

The right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism."

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country."

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.

"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation."

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.
