#850. Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd

Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United head coach will be at Liverpool on 22 November

"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."

Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.

The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.

He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.

The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.

Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.

So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?

"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.

Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator

Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino

Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?

Matheus Cunha's injury-time goal against Roma on 3 November sealed one of only three Manchester United victories in 15 games this season

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.

Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.

"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.

"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."

Diogo Dalot is consoled by Manchester United team-mate Joshua Zirkzee after being substituted during the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa

That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.

Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.

Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.

Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.

The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.

It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.

However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.

Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.

Liverpool and Man Utd fans give predictions ahead of Premier League match

Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.

The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.

He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.

For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.

Why does Pochettino keep lemons in his office?

Fernandes' status affects other areas. Carrick never seemed convinced by Andrey Santos, a Â£50m summer arrival from Chelsea. But with Â£70m Carlos Baleba out for an extended period, a partner needs to be found in midfield for Kobbie Mainoo.

Tielemans did not seem to have the running ability for the role, and Amorim wouldn't pick Mainoo with Fernandes.

Further forward, with Benjamin Sesko out, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo have tended to be used in the number nine role. But Cunha likes to drop deep, while, after a bright start to the season, Mbeumo has scored twice in his past 12 appearances.

Neither Shea Lacey nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Both caught the eye on England Under-20 duty during the international break. Pochettino has history for giving young players a chance and the pair could benefit from that.

Manchester United co-chair Avram Glazer and minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe have been the subject of numerous supporter protests and chants

There is one issue Pochettino mentioned in his interview he will soon discover requires delicate handling.

United's match-going fans have stood by every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. There is no reason to think that will change now.

However, their relationship with the club's ownership is fractured, possibly beyond repair. Fresh accounts to 30 September show the club's overall debt remains more than Â£1.1bn and a further Â£14.5m was spent on finance costs in the previous quarter.

This fuels discontent in the stands, already heightened because of various ticketing measures, none of which are viewed by most supporters as being positive.

"Chemistry is really important, chemistry between us and the staff and the fans and the players, the directors, the owners and everything."

#849. Summer signings join Lionel Messi among MLS’s top earners: Takeaways from the league’s salary release

How much in player salaries did it take to earn a point in the 2026 MLS regular season? The latest batch of salaries lends some insight

Lionel Messi has closer company at the top of MLS’s list of highest-paid players, thanks to another pair of former Barcelona attackers. The Inter Miami captain is still comfortably the league’s top earner, on a guaranteed compensation of $28.3m. Robert Lewandowski (Chicago Fire) and Antoine Griezmann (Orlando City) have entered the list with the second and third highest wages, while Atlanta United’s Breel Embolo, another summer signing, ranks fifth on a guaranteed compensation of $10.8m. Second-year LAFC forward Son Heung-min sits fourth on $11.2m.

Casimiro, who joined Messi in Miami at the end of his contract with Manchester United, is his team’s fourth top-earner with a guaranteed compensation of $3.54m. This comes after Miami announced his signing as a non-designated player to the surprise of some as the Brazilian arrived on a Bosman transfer rather than a loan-with-purchase, as Rodrigo De Paul had last summer, to keep Miami rules compliant. The MLS Players’ Association lists Casimiro on a base salary of $896,004.

All of these earnings figures were revealed as part of the MLS Players’ Association’s twice-a-year data dump, with the latter installment dropping hours before the league’s postseason commenced. While these figures don’t include transfer fees and therefore don’t tell the whole picture of a team’s investment in its roster, it’s a useful bit of insight in regards to how each team is spending on player wages.

Figures are players’ guaranteed compensation inclusive of base salary and all guaranteed bonuses; does not include marketing and other bonuses.

Thirteen of MLS’s 30 clubs have a new highest earner after a busy post-World Cup transfer window. Two – Anders Dreyer (San Diego, $3.6m) and Mateusz Bogusz (Houston, $2.5m) – rose to the top after the departure of a higher-paid teammate. Lozano overtook the injured Riqui Puig after arriving with the LA Galaxy on loan from San Diego. Lewandowski, Griezmann, and Embolo hold similar status, while Charlotte replaced Wilfried Zaha with Allan Saint-Maximin ($7.2m) earning nearly three times as much as the Crystal Palace great.

Other top-earners signed from beyond the league are Brais Méndez (Columbus, $5.2m), André Luiz (Kansas City, $3.3m), and Kai Wagner (Philadelphia, $1.6m). Two strikers who were traded within the league mid-season signed fresh terms that made them their new teams’ highest-paid players: Rafael Navarro (St. Louis, $4.95m) and Dejan Joveljic (Seattle, $3.7m).

The standout failure of the new big earners is Alexis Sánchez. The 37-year-old Chile legend came to North America this summer, joining CF Montréal and making 15 league appearances for the Quebecois club but failing to register a single goal or assist. His $2.97m guaranteed compensation makes up 24.6% of the team’s wage bill.

Griezmann’s arrival means that Messi no longer carries the largest share of any team’s wage bill, as Orlando has dedicated slightly more to the Frenchman (49.5%) than Miami has to the Argentinian (47.7%). Lewandowski narrowly trails by accounting for 47.3% of Chicago’s wage spending. Importantly, Messi’s contract includes add-ons; a portion of Apple TV subscriptions, merchandise sales through Adidas and Fanatics, and an optional ownership stake in Miami when he retires.

Other notable new wages include former Middlesbrough attacking midfielder Morgan Whittaker (Colorado, $2.0m), former Watford and Everton midfielder Abdoulaye Doucouré (Charlotte, $1.0m), former Manchester United left-back Tyrell Malacia (Cincinnati, $1.04m), former NYCFC playmaker Santi Rodríguez (Columbus, $3.9m), South Africa striker Lyle Foster (Houston, $1.8m), former Celtic striker Kyōgo Furuhashi (LA Galaxy, $1.1m), Tunisia winger Elias Saad (Nashville, $1.7m), former Leeds winger Jack Harrison (New England, $3.65m), Côte d’Ivoire winger Bénie Traoré (NYCFC, $2.5m), former Netherlands striker Vincent Janssen (Portland, $1.75m), Tunisia winger Elias Achouri (San Diego, $2.6m), Scotland goalkeeper Angus Gunn (San Jose, $1.6m), and Southampton loanee Damion Downs (St Louis, $1.6m).

While this exercise cannot confidently include every transfer fee paid, the timing of this year’s drop after the regular season’s end allows us to size up how teams spent on wages against the league table.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Does spending more equal success? There’s a degree of correlation there, but it’s not strong.

How valuable is it to get a point in MLS? In 2026’s wage economy, exactly $512,394.

#848. Washington Spirit v Kansas City Current: where the NWSL Championship will be won and lost

Croix Bethune, Trinity Rodman and the Rowdy Audi crowd are among the factors that could swing Saturday’s final

This year’s NWSL Championship blends recurring themes with some newness. For the familiar: the Washington Spirit are in the final for the third straight year, hoping the third time’s the charm after back-to-back 1-0 defeats in their past two attempts. Slightly familiar, too, is Kansas City Current playing the championship game at Washington’s Audi Field, where they lost the final to Portland in 2022 and where they will contend again Saturday.

For the novelty? Neither Kansas City nor Washington, despite their modern dominance in the NWSL table, have won the championship since 2021 (when Washington won). With Gotham’s bid for a two-peat stymied by the Current in the semi-final, here are five things that will decide a new winner in 2026.

Washington’s defensive pressure Washington have allowed the second-fewest goals in the NWSL this year. Through the season and into the playoffs, the center-back pairing of the English defender Esme Morgan and Tara Rudd, the Scottish goalkeeper Sandy MacIver (fourth-highest save percentage in NWSL) and the defensive midfielder Andi Sullivan have been tough to break through for even the league’s most elite attackers. Further up the field, the Spirit’s defense begins with an attacking unit fond of forcing mistakes that lead to goals, with the late-season addition of Clara Luvanga (who has seven goal contributions in seven games for the Spirit) a key impact.

Kansas City, who have scored more goals than any other NWSL team this year, will be a challenge. Defending set pieces will be a space to watch, as they provided the only goal Utah scored against the Spirit in the semi-final, and all the goals Kansas City scored against Gotham.

Bethune on a mission against former team This season’s Midfielder of the Year is representing a team in the NWSL Championship for the third straight year (her second with availability to play). But this will be her first not representing the Spirit. After leaving Washington for Missouri in February, Bethune is facing her former team for the chance to win her first championship trophy.

A bit more poetry: Bethune nearly broke the NWSL’s all-time single-season assists record during her 2024 rookie season for the Spirit. (A torn meniscus cut short her streak, but she still was named Rookie of the Year.) She finally broke it this season with Kansas City. Her creative influence in the Current’s midfield has been crucial to unlocking their goal-scoring capabilities. Bethune’s ability to pull apart Washington’s laudable defensive structure could prove crucial in the final.

Kansas City’s attacking depth Temwa Chawinga is a two-time NWSL MVP for a reason, but she wasn’t the sole source of Kansas City’s 54 goals in 30 regular season games. The Current’s past nine goals (across five games including the playoffs) were scored by six different players, with Haley Hopkins (tied with Chawinga for goal contributions in the regular season) notching four of them. Chawinga enters the Championship with only one goal contribution in five games and no goals since 3 October, but she can break through at any moment. If not, the Current’s surrounding cast of contributors – Hopkins, Michelle Cooper, Bethune and Debinha – seems prepared to make the difference.

Rodman is the Spirit’s gamechanger The Spirit also have attacking depth, but Rodman is a gamechanger whose impact is more lopsided. Her 20 goal contributions in the regular season were more than double the goal contributions of any teammate, and that’s without quantifying the space she frees up for fellow goalscorers with her calculated off-the-ball movements.

In the postseason, Rodman has four goal contributions in two games – two goals and two assists. Coming at the end of one of her best club seasons, a big performance in the final will be essential for a Spirit victory. It would also further solidify her as one of the deserved main characters (and highest-paid player) in the NWSL.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Will Rowdy Audi make a difference? Stadium squabbles were an unexpected storyline of this year’s postseason. Gotham and Washington faced scheduling hurdles that called into question their home-field advantage and/or forced them to play on less-than-ideal pitches for their semi-finals. But this Saturday, the Spirit will still have home-field advantage at Audi Field, where they’ve earned the trust of a robust home crowd. Whether Washington can turn that familiar, friendly space into the perfect scene for actually lifting the trophy in their third straight final would be a poetic end to the postseason’s stadium woes.

#846. How the Columbus Crew switched paths en route to the MLS playoffs

In a transformative year, Crew GM Issa Tall’s boldest change may have been to abandon his best-laid plans

The Columbus Crew have a more holistic operation than most in MLS. The club as a whole still exists thanks to the dogged efforts of their fervent fanbase that helped block relocation. Their under-19s won the national cup in June, while the developmental Crew 2 made a fourth semi-final berth in five seasons in MLS Next Pro. The first team regularly punches above its weight in MLS, winning the third-most major titles (nine) among MLS originals.

And yet, this year tested the conventions set by team and league alike.

In January, chief soccer officer Issa Tall welcomed the club’s eighth head coach, Henrik Rydström. Having only previously coached in his native Sweden, the 50-year-old used his introductory presser to laud the values of relationism, to praise his predecessor, and to plot a bold course for a new Crew. It was assumed he’d be around a while – the Crew have historically been patient with coaches, needing only seven bosses to navigate their first 30 seasons.

By mid-May, after just 16 games in charge, Rydström was on his way back to Sweden. His five wins were the lowest of the eight full-time Crew coaches. And yet, Saturday sees the Crew begin the MLS Cup Playoffs in a best-of-three matchup with Lionel Messi and Inter Miami.

Columbus are one of four teams to make the postseason following a midseason coaching change. Two of the other three could pin their turnarounds on players; Orlando City fired Óscar Pareja in March, but didn’t really shoot up the table until adding Antoine Griezmann after the World Cup. The Philadelphia Union surged thanks to interim coach, Ryan Richter, finally seeing if Cavan Sullivan could cut it in MLS (he can).

The Portland Timbers’ turnaround after sacking Phil Neville might be closest to Columbus’ story, though 2026 was his third season in the role. They weren’t at the start of a new path, and that path had not been decided after the departure of one of MLS’s most influential coaches to date: Wilfried Nancy.

“Wilfield had a huge impact on our club, and him departing is certainly not an easy thing to move on from,” Tall told the Guardian. “His time here was great for our club. But then there were things that we believed we could do better, whether it’s on the alignment of the scouting department, or even on the way the players are managed. There are ways you can evolve.”

Two Nancy acolytes seemed like obvious fits. One, Laurent Courtois, led the second team from 2022-2024 and had a brief sojourn as head coach of CF Montreal. Another, Yoann Damet, was Nancy’s top assistant and had long been earmarked as a head coach in the making. According to Tall, conversations with Damet left both coach and executive in a sense that it was best for Damet’s development to explore options beyond Columbus.

“At the end of the year, Yoann already had [done] some rounds [of interviews] with St Louis [City],” Tall said. “We all agreed that it’d be better for him to go to another club and become the head coach and the leader, as opposed to maybe always being seen as the former assistant coach”. Damet took that chance, setting up shop roughly 400 miles down I-70. His first season with St Louis has been transformative, leading the team to their first major trophy by winning the Lamar Hunt US Open Cup and finishing third in the West.

Despite determination to install a new coach before preseason kicked off in early January, Tall, technical director Marc Nicholls, and the rest of the Crew’s committee didn’t want to cut corners. Interviews were a three-stage process, with in-person conversations for the final round.

“The first one is really, ‘who are you’?” Tall said. “‘I’ve read about you, I’ve seen your team play, but what are your guiding principles as a person?’ In that first round you eliminate a lot of candidates because, based on the answer and maybe being egocentric or selfish, you can tell that they’re not a good fit.

“In the second round, you go more in-depth about the club and the coach. Then, third, is really going into deep details of everything in terms of preparations and so forth.”

Rydström seemed to fit the bill. Tall and Nancy had often admired his teams at Mälmo, which played with similar panache and kept the team punching above their weight class in the Allsvenskan. Conversations were productive, with Tall citing Mauricio Sarri’s Napoli sides as a shared inspiration.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

On 31 December, Tall and Rydström signed a pact – new year, new Crew. However, it was clear early on that the roster wasn’t adjusting as expected. Columbus took two points from their first five games, but the concerns were even more foundational – less Sarri, more sorry.

“I’ve been fortunate to be in many locker rooms, and I can feel the dynamic between players and staff,” Tall reflected. “If things don’t feel right, you could play the ostrich and pretend it’s okay. Give yourself another year and if it doesn’t work, it may be time to make a change.

“No, we couldn’t live with this. Seeing the lack of enthusiasm from the players, especially in-house, it begged for us to make a decision”. On 17 May, Rydström was relieved from his role. Courtois, who had joined Rydström as an assistant, quickly transitioned into taking the job he’d interviewed for, but now on an interim basis.

Tall cited this as a fair chance for Courtois to show what he could do in the role and pledged to back him in the transfer market. It took time, with the Crew losing five of his first eight games. But between the increased familiarity growing under his watch and a window which brought two crucial attackers (Brais Méndez and Santi Rodríguez) to Columbus, his team came out of the summer in far better shape than they’d entered it.

Since 1 September, no MLS team has racked up more points than Columbus’ 27. Courtois led the Crew to the Open Cup final, only to fall on penalties to Damet’s St Louis. So strong was their form that they bypassed the wild card game and finished in a guaranteed playoff place.

One would think Courtois has done all he can to prove he should, at long last, get the job on a permanent basis. Tall said those decisions would come after the team’s season ends but wasn’t shy about appreciating how much more the club resembled its usual self under Courtois’ stewardship. Seemingly the club’s sporting department might enjoy a more relaxed festive season this time around.

“It’s not just a ‘me’ decision, it’s a collective decision,” Tall stressed. “And, right now, we barely had time to breathe with all those games, and now being in the playoffs. But he’s done very well. I said that I would give him all the weapons for him to be successful, and the work done this summer, I think, was a testament to what I said.

“Nicholls, our technical director, was heavily involved in the signing of all of these players, very crucial. But when it comes to the future, it’s a discussion we’ll have when time allows. But yes, I think Laurent has a good shot to stay.”

#845. Fan found not guilty of racially abusing Semenyo

Antoine Semenyo was playing for Bournemouth when the alleged incident happened during a match against Liverpool in August 2025

A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing footballer Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the player withdrew his support for the prosecution.

Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool Magistrates' Court in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting racist abuse during the opening match of the Premier League season at Anfield on 15 August last year.

But Simon Jones, prosecuting, said: "Following recent contact made with Mr Semenyo, he has indicated he is no longer supportive of proceedings and the prosecution do not consider it is appropriate to compel him.

"In those circumstances we offer no further evidence in the case."

District Judge Mary Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty to the charge of racially aggravated behaviour.

Semenyo, who was a Bournemouth player at the time of the incident but is now signed for Manchester City, had been due to give evidence last month but the trial was adjourned halfway through when Mogan was taken to hospital after suffering a seizure.

Mark Mogan was accused of shouting abuse at Semenyo as he prepared to take a throw in

The court had heard that Mogan, in a wheelchair, shouted at Semenyo as he went to take a throw-in about 30 minutes into the game.

As he was preparing to take the throw-in Mogan allegedly shouted a racist insult.

Opening the case last month, Jones said: "That racial abuse was shouted directly at Antoine Semenyo, who was close to him.

"Mr Semenyo briefly froze, as he couldn't believe what the male had said."

Witnesses also said they saw him throw his chewing gum at the footballer.

Semenyo reported the incident to the match referee and Mogan was removed from the stadium at half-time.

Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police in an interview that Semenyo had called him a cripple after he shouted at the player to "hurry up".

Mogan, of Templehill Close in Dovecot, Liverpool, declined to comment as he left court.

#844. Maine Road offer non-league haven to fans of scandal-hit Manchester City

Tenth-tier club aim to become a new home for disillusioned supporters and those priced out of the Premier League

It began with a timely message on social media. “We’ve seen the posts. We’ve read the comments. If all the recent conversation has made you curious about the other team in Manchester playing in sky blue, come and see us.”

It was a direct response to the news of a guilty verdict in the Premier League’s financial fair play case against Manchester City and it came from the 10th-tier (step six) club Maine Road, who carry City’s colours and a near-identical badge, as well as the name of City’s previous home.

Maine Road stadium was demolished in 2003-04 and replaced by houses but two miles away, in a corner of Chorlton-cum-Hardy, Maine Road FC are playing in front of about 100 people on a cool November Saturday. The high-stakes surroundings of the Premier League seem a fair distance away, but Maine Road – founded in 1955 in Rusholme as a Manchester City supporters’ club team – have never professed to be City.

“There is FC United and Manchester United, who are intrinsically linked in terms of why that club exists,” says Rob McKay, Maine Road women’s head coach, watching as a fan as the men’s side draw 0-0 with Halewood Apollo in the North West Counties League First Division North. “This is not a protest club. The links with City have ebbed and flowed over the years. It’s just that they were playing out of the Maine Road social club when it formed.”

The chair and director Alex Simmonds, who arrived in the summer, has big ambitions for Maine Road. He believes the fallout from City’s legal battle with the Premier League could help attract a new audience.

“It was a bit of a statement,” Simmonds says of that social media post. “We came across a lot of comments when the news came out and a lot were saying: ‘Well, we’ll stop watching City if they get relegated or if anything happens, and we’ll just go to Maine Road.’ That came up in quite a few conversations online.”

Simmonds admits there has not yet been a huge rise in crowd numbers, with City fans, perhaps understandably, staying defiantly loyal to their club, who have appealed against the independent commission’s verdict. His priority is to regenerate Maine Road. “For me coming into the club, it was about trying to get people to see that we are here,” he says. “To get in touch with the community and to get fans down here, so no matter who you support in the Premier League or Championship or whatever, we are here.”

Maine Road offer free entry to anyone with a season ticket for a Premier League or EFL club, hoping to boost numbers during international breaks or when other Greater Manchester teams play away. Simmonds is helping to fund a multimillion-pound renovation of St Margaret’s Community Centre, which serves as Maine Road’s clubhouse. The club are also launching a new website and a scheme to hand out thousands of free tickets to local primary schools.

Will that, combined with potential disillusionment after any City punishment, bring fans flocking to Maine Road? “I think it will,” Simmonds says, “but only if people know that there’s a difference between a Premier League Man City and a Maine Road at step six. If they come with ideas that we are going to be a City or even one of the bigger semi-pro teams … we’re not quite there yet. But their support would help.”

Non-league football in Greater Manchester has enjoyed a significant surge in popularity since Covid, so Maine Road find themselves in a crowded marketplace. McKay says: “West Didsbury and Chorlton are down the road and they get 1,000. Droylsden get huge crowds, Ashton United get huge crowds, Curzon Ashton are getting reasonable crowds. There’s so much football.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Simmonds believes the connection with City, however loose, should help Maine Road gradually gain a foothold. City’s former training ground at Platt Lane is a stone’s throw from Brantingham Road, where Maine Road play. City’s academy teams have played at Maine Road’s ground, as well as at nearby St Bede’s College.

Another connection is the fact Maine Road are managed by a former City player in Leon Mike, who made his only City start at the old Maine Road in 2001 under Kevin Keegan.

“People make jokes about the Etihad not being full, but genuinely, a lot of times you speak to City fans, they’ll say it’s too expensive,” says Mike. “Premier League, FA Cup, League Cup, Champions League, that’s a lot of games to go to. Whereas on a Saturday here it will cost you £6 to attend and you can have a pint and some food.”

There is optimism among those most closely connected with Maine Road that the club will soon experience growth. “We gained 9,000 followers across the platforms just on the back of that one social media post,” Simmonds says. “It was surprising – I didn’t think it would do that – but social media is really powerful. We’re definitely going to try and stay in that conversation and get people coming through.”

#843. Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator

New Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino (right) worked with his full squad for the first time on Thursday

Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.

Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded on to YouTube.

Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.

The drone operator, who initially defended their use of filming the session, has since deleted the footage and apologised for uploading it.

"A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Manchester United training session at Carrington. Whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part," said the drone operator.

"I had wrongly presumed that with it being close to the start of the session that no meaningful training sessions would have started, so would have been some harmless warming up shown.

"I would also like to state that Liverpool Football Club or any other football club were not involved in my decision to film at Carrington yesterday."

Manchester United face rivals Liverpool at Anfield on 22 November.

Manchester United have declined to comment.

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino (second right) hugs forward Bryan Mbeumo

There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.

While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, and neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Jaume Camacho 17, who is yet to feature at senior level, was also with the group.

On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.

Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.

The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.

Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

#841. Race for the Fifa presidency: lineup revealed to challenge Gianni Infantino

Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima are both standing

But Ramon Vega fails to get the necessary backing

Fifa has confirmed that Gianni Infantino will face challenges from Philippe Diallo of France and Japan’s Kozo Tashima in March’s presidential election.

The president of the French football federation and the honorary president of the Japan football association submitted nomination letters with endorsements from five member associations by Wednesday night’s midnight CET deadline. The former Switzerland and Tottenham defender Ramon Vega has not met that threshold, despite repeatedly saying he would stand.

“The candidatures have been forwarded to the electoral committee for examination and for passing a decision on the admission of the candidate,” Fifa said.

The election in Rabat on 18 March will be the first time Infantino has faced opposition since he was first elected in 2016, when he defeated the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) president, Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa, by 115 votes to 88.

Infantino had been expected to be re-elected unopposed for a third time after declaring his candidacy in April and had received more than 200 letters of endorsement from national associations by the time of last summer’s World Cup, but the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise plan has led to a haemorrhaging of support.

Uefa has led a campaign to unseat him since July with backing from Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, and initially the AFC, but with Infantino conducting a global tour to rally support from smaller nations the opposition has struggled to put up an alternative candidate.

Tashima was the first to declare last month in defiance of the AFC, which after criticising the FFE proposal is backing Infantino, having come under pressure from the region’s two major financial powerhouses, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

As revealed by the Guardian on Monday, Diallo was belatedly chosen last weekend as the Uefa candidate after a complex selection process. The 63-year-old’s emergence was a surprise because Uefa had initially hoped to field a more high-profile candidate, such as Arsène Wenger. The Hungarian banker Sandor Csanyi, the president of his country’s FA, had strong backers owing to his close relationship with Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Diallo and Tashima may yet join forces in an attempt to defeat Infantino amid concerns of splitting those opposed to the president among the 211 Fifa members. Were that to occur it is expected Tashima would stand aside, a development that would be supported by Uefa.

All three candidates will be vetted by Fifa’s governance, audit and compliance committee, chaired by the Infantino ally Bruno Chiomento, before the nominations are confirmed on 18 February.

#840. Germany news: Parliament agrees on debt-laden 2027 budget

The budget committee in the Bundestag worked into the night to sign off on next year's spending plans. These include levels of new debt only eclipsed once, at the height of the COVID pandemic.

These updates have been closed. Below, you can review our collection of news and analysis on stories from or relating to Germany from Friday, November 13.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz got a birthday cake at the UN climate summit in Turkey this week. But he wasn't there to eat it. Meanwhile, in Berlin, climate activists marked his 71st birthday on Friday with a symbolic chocolate cake. Their message: they too want to reach that age on a livable planet.

Fridays for Future is taking its demands to German streets. Demonstrations were planned in more than 70 German cities on Friday, November 13.

Under the slogan "Pay your climate debt," protesters in the German capital demanded more funding for climate protection and adaptation in developing countries, alongside a global phase-out of coal, oil and gas.

Germany provided €4.7 billion ($5.2 billion) in federal budget funds for international climate financing in 2025 — below its €6 billion pledge.

But the protest movement is no longer drawing the crowds it once did. In September 2019, Fridays for Future mobilized an estimated 1.4 million people across Germany. Five years later, that figure fell to around 75,000 at a comparable nationwide strike.

This comes as broader youth frustration with German politics grows. "I don't feel addressed by the chancellor unfortunately," Kim, a protester in Berlin, told DW.

From military service to affordable housing and climate policy, younger Germans are questioning whether their concerns are being heard.

A recent nationwide poll found that 82% of Germans believe politicians do not adequately represent young people's interests. Among 18- to 34-year-olds, just 5% trust Merz's conservatives to champion their concerns, compared with 3% for their Social Democratic coalition partners.

Merz is not the first German chancellor to miss a UN climate summit. And smaller demonstrations do not necessarily mean young Germans care less about climate change. But the contrast is striking: while the climate movement struggles to mobilize, dissatisfaction among younger voters extends well beyond environmental policy.

Julian Reichelt, formerly the editor-in-chief of Germany's top-selling tabloid Bild, says he was the target of an arson attack after his car was set on fire and largely destroyed in Berlin.

Now editor-in-chief of the right-wing online portal Nius that he co-founded, Reichelt said the arson attack took place in the Charlottenburg district of the German capital overnight.

Police confirmed the car was intentionally set alight, saying a passerby reported it shortly after 2 a.m. that morning. However, they did not name a suspect or potential personal motive at first, saying only that the fire department responded and extinguished the fire.

"It is completely clear that this was a targeted attack," Reichelt said, calling it an "attempt at intimidation against new free media that stand up against this left-wing extremism."

Similar arson attacks several years ago targeted cars belonging to a columnist for another Berlin newspaper, B.Z., with a left-wing group claiming responsibility in one case.

That said, Berlin also has a more general and fairly well documented problem with arson and vandalism targeting cars, with an average of roughly two a night being set alight in the capital city over recent years. Vandalism and insurance fraud are the most common reasons more generally.

Reichelt was fired from his prominent job at Bild in 2021 amid allegations of sexual harassment, accusations he always denied and referred to as a "smear campaign."

Lawmakers in the Bundestag have approved reforms that will provide additional powers to Germany's domestic and external intelligence agencies.

The changes will strengthen both the external Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and domestic intelligence service the BfV, formally titled the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

The law passed fairly comfortably in the federal Bundestag lower house of parliament, with 309 votes in favor, 190 against and 71 abstentions.

The BfV will be granted powers beyond intelligence gathering and monitoring individuals, such as being able to secretly enter homes or take action against explosives or weapons.

In the case of the BND, it will be granted additional operational intervention powers, for instance moving to disable servers belonging to state-sponsored hacker groups abroad.

The changes aim to respond to intensified and evolving threats from foreign intelligence services and their partners, and to reduce dependency on information supplied by friendly foreign intelligence services.

Opposition parties have accused the government of abolishing or weakening the separation between the police and intelligence services — a sensitive and closely monitored distinction in German society, because of the legacy both of Adolf Hitler's Nazi regime and of the secret police services in Communist East Germany during the Cold War.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Friedrich Merz has said during his visit to Dublin that Germany and Europe's position in future peace talks for Ukraine is "set."

Following the talks in Abu Dhabi this week between Ukraine and Russia brokered by the US, which also involved European representatives at times, Merz said further negotiations were now planned.

"In the coming weeks there should now be concrete peace talks in which Europe is represented," Merz told reporters in Dublin amid an informal meeting of EU leaders.

He said that "provisionally" this might involve the same "group of Europeans" who had participated in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"Germany is set in there, that is completely clear," he said.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's call to link EU budget negotiations to the provision of assistance to Ukraine, which faced hefty criticism at home, has found some backing amid European Political Community meetings and an AI summit in Dublin.

Merz, who has been leading the charge to find savings in the next EU budget, said doing so could ensure stronger contributions to helping Ukraine from all EU member states.

Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal said during the meeting in Dublin that he approved of Merz's suggestion "that support for Ukraine is also a part of our core security and our core financing."

He said that members who wanted a new EU budget should contribute.

Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, meanwhile, said he agreed completely with Merz.

"We must all pull in the same direction. All of Europe must do its part," he said.

Luxembourg's Luc Frieden also said that "we must all stand behind Ukraine" and added that collective financial commitments should be a part of this.

As the largest economy and most populous country in the EU, Germany is the largest overall contributor both to the EU budget and to assistance for Ukraine.

Countries that tend to be so-called net beneficiaries of the EU budget, rather than net contributors to it, tend to be more reticent to cut spending plans.

Hosts Ireland, in a tricky position as the holders of the rotating presidency of the EU trying to broker a deal on the next seven-year budget, said it had concerns about adding an additional factor to the stalled talks, as the current budget's expiry at the end of 2027 starts to draw near.

"But I do understand why this is happening," Taoiseach (or prime minister) Micheal Martin said in Dublin. "Some countries have made considerable contributions and they want all EU member states to contribute financially to the support for Ukraine."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) was critical of both the spending and the fundraising plans in the 2027 budget, claiming without showing its workings that it would be able to do more with less by making swingeing cuts in various key areas.

Budget policy spokesman Michael Espendiller said the budget meant "more debts and more taxes and more burdens for the taxpayer."

He accused the Christian Democrats of breaking key election pledges by raising taxes on alcohol and tobacco. He then complained that despite this, there was not enough money for the promised electricity tax cut.

"If you put it into figures, the federal government will be taking out almost €400,000 (around $440,000) every minute in new debt," Espendiller said, calling for an end to what he called a spiral of debt.

He claimed that the AfD would have able to complete its budget with new debt of just €63 billion, not roughly €210 billion, while simultaneously providing tax relief of around €44 billion.

Espendiller said this would be achieved with wide-reaching cuts in several core areas of spending: climate protection, contributing to the EU budget and other EU funding, asylum-related spending, international development aid, and weapons deliveries and other assistance to Ukraine.

It's unclear to what extent these proposed cuts would be feasible or legal, or what domestic or international implications they might have, or whether they'd save anything like the amount the AfD asserts in practice.

Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

The session took over 15 hours, and already politicians are talking about areas where they still see room for further improvement or alteration — but the document does at least stand in such a form in which it can take effect without too many complications.

Including all spending plans, in the core budget and from the so-called "special funds" for infrastructure and military modernization, new debt constitutes around a third of oultays.

In total, the plan is to take out new debt worth just over €210 billion ($233 billion), while taking in a little less than €400 billion in taxes.

That's the second-highest level of new debt in the post-war history of the Federal Republic of Germany. Even at the height of the COVID pandemic in 2021, new debt was only slightly higher, at €215.4 billion.

We'll likely be returning to the various details of and reactions to this story throughout the morning.

The environmentalist Greens took aim at Chancellor Merz for not delivering on a promise to reduce taxes on electricity in the final budget.

"The big promise that Chancellor Merz made a few days ago, sinking electricity taxes for everyone, this promise remains a broken promise," party co-leader Britta Hasselmann said on ZDF television on Friday.

"It was possible to find a way at short notice for several other things in this budget," she said.

"I think this demonstrates the inadequate planning and the weak leadership of the chancellor," Hasselmann said.

She added that the CDU forcing a delay to the planned sugar tax at short notice was further evidence of the planning shortcomings.

A budget expert at the party, Sebastian Schäfer, similarly alleged a "leadership vacuum in this coalition government," saying that what was put forward was less a budget and more a "wooden shack wihtout foundations."

The Left Party's budget policy spokesman Dietmar Bartsch has lamented a "knot garden of debt, tricks and delays," accusing the coalition of not conducting "responsible budgetary policy."

Despite criticizing the debt levels, Bartsch also said it was "deeply unserious" to float electricity tax relief but then withdraw the plan.

He said this would have cost less money than the federal government's plan to buy a share of the arms company KNDS. He also said it was unacceptable for the center-left Social Democrats to be celebrating just because "the odd welfare cut is not happening."

Ines Schwerdtner, co-leader of the party that firmly opposes defense spending and is at best lukewarm on NATO membership, said the record spending showed that money was not as tight as Merz's government made out.

"The debt brake is suspended for weapons, but for housing and electricity taxes they scrimp for every euro," Schwerdtner said. "The money is there, this government is just distributing it completely incorrectly."

Schwerdtner, herself a member of the budget committed in the Bundestag, called it a "budget of naivete."

More on this morning's top story in Berlin, the 2027 budget being signed off.

As the CDU calls for further savings, the Social Democrats say that the energy tax relief recently touted by Chancellor Friedrich Merz "would have to be financed with additional debts."

Ahead of Thursday's marathon talks, Merz had said he hoped to introduce the tax relief amid the stress caused by issues including the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

The SPD's Dirk Wiese said the junior coalition partners were "not disinclined to pave the way for the electricity tax relief," but not by making cuts elsewhere.

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the SPD had said he did not see enough fiscal wiggle room to enable the desired tax break.

Bremen's mayor Andreas Bovenshulte, also a Social Democrat, said that while he would have welcomed the relief, other decisions meant it wasn't possible.

"For that, a serious financing source would have been required, for instance with a plastic or sugar of windfall tax," Bovenschulte said, in reference to either delayed or proposed but rejected plans to potentially increase tax revenues.

German defense industry startup Quantum Systems said its drones were operational worldwide once again, including with the Bundeswehr military, after a cyberattack by "hostile actors" last month.

The company had announced the cyberattack on Thursday, amid reporting from the Financial Times that also said the Bundeswehr had grounded its drones from the company.

"The fleet is operating normally around the globe — including Germany and the Bundeswehr," a Quantum Systems spokesperson said in an emailed statement to the Reuters news agency. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution."

The company, based near Munich, had earlier said it uncovered an "active cyberattack" by hostile actors.

"The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said in a statement, adding there was no risk for end users and operators using its unmanned systems.

Quantum drones are used by Ukrainian armed forces in their defensive war against Russia, among others.

"Companies at the forefront of supporting Ukraine are being targeted precisely because our work is critically relevant to customers' security," the company said. "Being aware of this responsibility, Quantum Systems has mitigation plans in place and strives to fulfil the highest standard of data and system security."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Senior Christian Democrat Union (CDU) politician Matthias Middelberg appeared on ZDF television this morning to discuss the budget breakthrough.

He identified one "weak point" after the overnight negotiations.

"We have not yet saved enough, we still need to save a lot more," he said.

Middelberg said that in his view the government would not be able to "collect the funds," because that would put too much tax strain on people and businesses.

Therefore, he said, "the government must make cutbacks."

Middelberg acepted that it wasn't clear how to do this, speculating that "perhaps there are subsidies or some other things" that could be ripe to be trimmed.

He said the leadership of the coalition government's CDU/CSU and Social Democrats would "consider this question very closely once more."

The German government statistics agency Destatis has published new figures on insolvency filings for the month of August.

A total of 2,067 companies registered insolvencies with German courts during the month, Destatis said, 4.4% more than in the same month in 2025.

The data operates on something of a delay, because the government tracks when courts grant the status, which can be almost three months after the initial application at times.

The increase has been a rolling trend this year. From January to August, 17,252 companies have filed for insolvency, 6.6% more than in the same period last year.

However, the total sum of debts forgiven in insolvency proceedings is actually quite considerably lower than in the first eight months of last year, at €25.9 billion ($28.7 billion) rather than €37.2 billion, because fewer large companies have gone bust.

More individuals are also filing for bankruptcy protection than in 2025, although the rise is somewhat less sharp. In August, 6,301 people gained insolvency protection, 2.8% more than last August. For January through August, the year-on-year increase is more modest, at 1.2%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

Moin! Here's hoping you slept more and better than the Bundestag's budget committee. Or if not, at least let's hope that you had more fun.

Its members worked towards the dawn in a session lasting over 15 hours, trying to iron out the last wrinkles in spending plans for 2027.

The proverbial white smoke emerged at around 6 in the morning in Berlin, with word of a finalized agreement.

If you were tired of talk and criticism of the "debt brake" and the "black zero" (a promise not to take any new debts) in the years following the eurozone debt crisis, rest assured we can assign such chatter to the history books for now.

The borrowing plans for 2027 — if you incorporate new debt taken out as part of so-called "special funds," for instance for the military and infrastructure, rather than as part of the core budget — are the second highest in the history of post-war Germany.

The country only took out more new debt in 2021, at the height of the COVID pandemic and even then it was very close indeed.

We'll bring you more news and reactions on this, and whatever else breaks around the country, as Friday develops.

#839. How Premier League's big six keep getting richer

Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'big six' clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.

We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was Â£120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to Â£442m.

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."

Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.

It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or Â£713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned Â£37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool Â£35.5m and Chelsea Â£33.3m. Newcastle received only Â£13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

Their value pillar is projected to be worth Â£25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.

Not just by a small amount. They were Â£74m behind Tottenham, and Â£200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.

City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals.

City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors.

The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.

Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of Â£80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."

Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only Â£16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by Â£69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by Â£85m.

"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."

Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.

"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't."

The big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.

This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.

"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said.

"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues."

Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.

If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.

Premier League clubs spent Â£3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the Â£3.53bn set in 2025-26.

The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.

"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said.

"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under Â£100m."

Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.

In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.

Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than Â£40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.

So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.

And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.

Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.

They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.

Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.

But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.

"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.

"The big six can afford to make signings which are Â£60m and Â£70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years."

And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.

The commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.

Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending Â£945m on players in the past five years.

The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.

But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.

And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

#838. Mauricio Pochettino calls for Manchester United to show no fear against Liverpool

New head coach’s first game is at Anfield on Sunday

‘We are going there with the idea to win and be brave’

Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start.

United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach will not accept any self-doubt. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and is keen to instil those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick.

“We are going to Anfield with the idea to win and be brave and to be Manchester United,” Pochettino told the club’s website. “The history talks for us, and what we need to expect. We need to be sure that we are brave and we are protagonists and go there with no fears and challenge a very good team like Liverpool.”

Pochettino arrived in Manchester on Wednesday after an overnight flight, having taken charge of his final USA match against Haiti. He toured the training ground and held meetings with senior staff and players not on international duty.

Members of Pochettino’s staff were in place earlier in the week as they seek to revitalise a team with one league win. Pochettino is waiting for United to ratify the appointment of Sílvia Tuyà, a strength and conditioning coach who worked with him with the USA. She travelled with him by private jet to Manchester but was not named among the staff later in the day.

“We need to go little by little, step by step,” Pochettino said. “We cannot go too fast but also we need to, at the same time, attack the priorities to build something.”

He said it was important he and his staff adapt to the culture of the club. “And then, with this sense of knowing the history of the club, try to create all together, because we are all different, a culture, a philosophy that can respect that identity, the history of the club. But at the same time, performing. If we don’t perform, the responsibility is mine.”

Pochettino has coveted the United job and is a keen admirer of Sir Alex Ferguson, whom he describes as “the best coach in history”. Since the Scot’s retirement in 2013, United have failed to match his success but Pochettino said he was looking at “the potential of the club”. The weight of past achievements has hindered individuals over the past 13 years.

“The players need to express their talent,” Pochettino said. “We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now: it’s to work with them and try to take the pressure.

“Pressure needs to bring energy, responsibility needs to bring energy. Because if not, it’s too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back. When you connect with the game, you connect through your talent when you feel freedom, when you feel happy, when you want to play for your teammates, when you want to play for your family, when you want to play for your club, your fans.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

He sounded an upbeat note, saying: “With the power of this club and the fans supporting us, I think we will get in the place that we deserve to be.”

United’s total borrowings have risen to £784.5m, with long-term debt up by almost £100m over the past year. Figures published for the three months to 30 September show long-term borrowings of £577.4m, compared with £481.2m 12 months earlier. United’s cash reserves fell from £80.5m to £55.5m during the same period despite an increase in revenue.

The club reported a quarterly net loss of £18.1m, compared with £6.6m ​in ​the same period a year earlier. Revenue rose by 4% to £146m.

#837. Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue

Manchester City have won the Premier League on eight occasions

Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors if any of Manchester City's sponsors sue them.

The clubs met in London on Thursday for the first time since City were found guilty of a catalogue of charges relating to the breaching of the league's financial rules by an independent commission in September.

City have appealed and maintain their innocence, with a sanction yet to be decided.

The club's sponsors Etihad and Etisalat have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League.

At present, under the league's articles of association, a director is financially covered if they win a legal case brought against them by a third party, but not if they lose. The league's rules will now be updated to extend legal indemnity for chief executive Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittan and three other non-executive directors.

City and Nottingham Forest were the only two clubs that voted against the proposal to provide extra legal protection, with the other 18 clubs voting in favour.

Due to collective responsibility, it means that all clubs are now liable to cover legal costs that could run into hundreds of millions of pounds, raising the intriguing possibility of City being financially impacted by the legal action of its own sponsors.

BBC Sport was told that City's CFO Ingo Bank asked Premier League chair Brittan during Thursday's meeting if the proposal was a direct result of threats of legal action from Etihad and Etisalat, but she said she could not comment.

While Forest have declined to comment, their objection to the proposal is said have to been on procedural grounds, rather than due to any support for City.

The club did not believe that sufficient information had been provided, or adequate time afforded, for clubs to properly consider the implications of the proposed amendment, particularly given the potentially significant financial responsibilities involved. It felt that such a decision warranted more scrutiny and informed consideration before clubs were asked to vote.

An independent commission appointed by the Premier League found City guilty of artificially inflating the club's revenues by over Â£830m over a nine-year period in September.

The commission determined that the club arranged "sham" contracts with sponsors, which disguised funding from club owners the Abu Dhabi United Group.

Premier League CEO Masters said City "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade".

In October, City sponsor Etihad Airways said it was considering legal action against the Premier League.

In a statement, the United Arab Emirates-based airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etisalat signalled its intention to follow suit earlier this month and described the Premier League's verdict as "entirely false and defamatory".

#836. Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year

Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.

Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.

The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.

The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.

Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.

"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.

"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."

The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.

The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).

Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.

Sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Meet the SPOTY Men's Footballer of the Year contenders

Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.

In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.

That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.

Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.

The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.

Bellingham was recently joined in the England squad by his brother Jobe

In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.

His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.

Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.

Kane scored his first England goal 79 seconds into his debut in 2015

Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.

The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.

Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.

It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.

Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.

He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.

Mbappe has won eight consecutive league golden boots

Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.

By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.

His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.

Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.

His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.

Rodri scored the goal that won Manchester City the Champions League in 2023

Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.

For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.

At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.

He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

Lamine Yamal was 16 years and 362 days when he scored at the European Championship in 2024
