#835. Premier League clubs vote through new rules to increase legal protection for board

Individual indemnity extended for potential lawsuits

Key figures may be named in action over Manchester City

Clubs rallied behind the Premier League’s leadership in a key vote on Thursday, overwhelmingly backing new rules that would protect the chief executive, Richard Masters, from potentially damaging lawsuits.

A vote to expand the legal indemnity afforded to Premier League directors was won 18-2 at a shareholders’ meeting in central London, granting Masters and other figures greater protection in the event they were subjected to legal action as a consequence of doing their job.

Manchester City are understood to be one of two clubs to vote against the extension of indemnity, and one unnamed side spoke out at length against the measures during the meeting. The other vote against was by Nottingham Forest, who felt insufficient time had been granted to consider the proposal.

The rule change follows reports that the organisation’s leadership may be named in possible legal action by City’s Abu Dhabi sponsors, who have claimed their reputations were damaged as a result of the excoriating verdict of an independent commission regarding City’s breaches of the league’s financial rules. City have appealed against the verdict.

This week the Abu Dhabi telecommunications giant and City sponsor Etisalat released a statement describing the contents of the verdict as “entirely false and defamatory”. Referring to the independent commission’s report as “the published findings of the English Premier League”, Etisalat said it was “actively considering all options relating to its rights and associated legal remedies in this matter”.

The details of any increase of indemnity, including who would cover any potential costs, were not discussed in the meeting.

The chief refereeing officer of Pro Ref, Howard Webb, attended and came under sustained questioning from club executives over recent referee and video assistant referee failures.

A report by the independent key match incidents panel this week found there had been two serious mistakes that were not corrected by the VAR during the most recent round of matches. Webb is understood to have acknowledged that performance in matchday 10 had been “poor” but argued that apart from that weekend, key metrics on decision-making had been trending in the right direction this season.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The Premier League has confirmed next season will begin on Friday 13 August and finish on 21 May. It said players would have 75 “clear days” of break at the end of the current season.

#833. OL Lyonnes show their class to hit Arsenal’s ambitions for a top-four WCL finish

Arsenal’s hopes of earning automatic progression to the Champions League quarter-finals were dashed by OL Lyonnes, as the French side continued their statement form in Europe.

Goals in either half from Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay were the ­difference at Meadow Park and Lyonnes are joint-top of the table and still yet to concede in the league phase with one game remaining.

It feels like Lyonnes are playing with a fire and intensity fuelled by their loss to Barcelona in May’s Champions League final. They look a more formidable, coherent and hungry side on a mission to end a four-year run without lifting the trophy they won eight times in a 12-year period between 2011 and 2022.

“We are already at a better level for sure,” said the Lyonnes manager ­Jonatan Giráldez. “Sometimes you just need time. We had nine new ­players last season and I was new too as the coach. I think we have improved the rhythm of the game and have identified positions better and are staying more compact. The most important thing is speaking the same language in possession and out possession.”

The visit of the eight-time ­European champions was always going to be challenging for the ­Gunners and based on current form getting a result would be even tougher. Last season’s runners-up had scored 20 goals without conceding in their first four Champions League matches prior to their trip to Borehamwood and scored 49 in their nine Première Ligue games.

The lack of competitiveness in the France top flight also meant they were able to rotate heavily at the weekend between their two European games. Giráldez made 11 changes for their 1-0 defeat of Saint-Malo on Saturday before returning to his first-choice lineup against the 2025 Champions League winners.

Clàudia Pina scored a hat-trick as Barcelona thrashed Servette 6-0 to go top of the Women’s Champions League standings. While Lyon were winning 2-0 at Arsenal, Barça edged clear at the top on goal difference as they dismantled their Swiss visitors.

Aitana Bonmatí fired in the opener in the 19th minute and then turned provider for Pina to drill home her first goal.

Esmee Brugts headed in a third in the 32nd minute, and Barça had their fourth just after the hour, with Caroline Graham Hansen hitting an emphatic penalty after Bénédicte Simon fouled Brugts.

Pina got her second in the 77th minute and tucked in from Brugts’s pull-back to complete her hat-trick late on.

Bayern Munich are two points behind after cruising to a 4-0 win over Austria Vienna. Klara Buhl headed the visitors in front after 27 minutes before Pernille Harder doubled the lead in first-half stoppage time.

Alara Sehitler’s stunning strike made it 3-0 with 15 minutes to go before Sophie Proost added a fourth in stoppage time.

Sofia Jahnukainen struck in stoppage time as Roma snatched a 3-2 win away to Benfica. Kayleigh van Dooren twice put the Italians in front, but her first goal was cancelled out by a thunderbolt from Caroline Møller, with Flourish Sabastine equalising after her second.

Paris FC got their first win of the competition, beating HB Køge 2-1 thanks to Célina Ould Hocine’s late penalty. Catherine Paulson fired the visitors in front 10 minutes in, but Sheika Scott bundled in a rebound to bring Paris level before the break. Press Association

Arsenal were not afforded the ­luxury of an easy league match after their battling 1-1 draw against ­Barcelona last week, playing a critical and tricky game against London City Lionesses, which also ended 1-1. Renée Slegers made two changes to the team that hosted ambitious London City, with Ona Batlle ­having picked up a knock Taylor Hinds played at left-back and Kyra Cooney-Cross started ahead of Kim Little.

They had their backs against the wall at a bitterly cold Meadow Park, as Giráldez’s galacticos controlled the game. The away team had almost 69% possession in the first half and amassed 12 shots to Arsenal’s one.

The surprise was that Lyonnes were not further ahead at the break, with Brand’s 24th-minute goal the difference, the full-back sweeping in Vicki Bècho’s ball from the right.

Brand was back to haunt the ­Gunners, having scored in both legs of last season’s semi-final between the two teams, with the French side progressing to face Barcelona in the final with a 4-3 aggregate win.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Arsenal were better after the break, but Lyonnes soaked up brief spells of Arsenal pressure, Marie-Antoinette Katoto the only player left forward as they banked back and crowded the box to give the home players few options.

They increased their margin and dampened the mood soon after Arsenal’s brightest period, Tabitha Chawinga’s cross from the left was collected by Katoto and the France forward laid the ball off for Dumornay who took a touch before powering the ball into the roof of the net.

It was an emphatic and unstoppable finish from one of the best players in the world as a mist lowered over the pitch.

“Congratulations to Lyonnes, they were better than us today,” said Slegers. “If you look at the block we’ve had, the challenges we’ve had with the run of games – ­Liverpool and Barcelona away, ­London City who are among one of the top teams in the WSL right now and Lyon, who are even better than last year – it’s a lot of games against strong teams with a short turnaround because Lyon were better than us.”

Arsenal need to quickly move on, with West Ham their last game before the international break. They had needed a win to have any serious chance of earning a place in top four, avoiding a quarter-final playoff place.

They now sit eighth and will face Inter in their final league phase match in December, with the Italians needing a win to keep any hopes of a playoff place alive. That will not be easy, but a seeded playoff place is in Arsenal’s hands, if they want it.

#832. Thomas Frank admits he has a point to prove after taking reins at Crystal Palace

‘I know what I want and the direction we should go in’

Thomas Frank has admitted he has a point to prove on his return to management as he aims to steer Crystal Palace away from relegation trouble after taking over from Pierre Sage.

The Dane was confirmed as manager on Monday with Palace at the bottom of the table after 10 matches having conceded 24 goals – the most in the Premier League. They face a crucial trip to Coventry on Saturday and Frank said he had been “surprised about how good it feels” after returning to work for the first time since being sacked by ­Tottenham in February.

The 53-year-old spent most of the intervening period travelling, working as a pundit at the World Cup and taking in trips to Japan, Australia and his native Denmark, where he was visiting friends and family when he received the SOS call from Palace last week. Frank previously spent seven years in charge of Brentford but left Spurs after just eight months with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history. He believes he has learned from that experience.

“I think you’ve all got an ego,” he said. “Some are better at controlling it than others. For me, it’s not the critics. It’s more what I can bring myself, what I can learn, what I can prove, how I can get better. I think that’s the big thing.

“In this world there’s a lot of clever people out there. But they only know a 10th of the truth. And that’s a 10th of the truth at Brentford and a 10th of the truth at Tottenham. That’s just the way it is – if you can’t handle that as a coach or a player or whatever, then you shouldn’t be in this business. I’m just very happy to be back in the game, very happy to be in a fantastic club, at Palace, where you walk in the door and you just feel the energy. You feel the people. It just feels good.”

Frank said he is planning to pick Roy Hodgson’s brains in the coming days after recalling a conversation they had when the former England and Palace manager was still at Selhurst Park.

“I was thinking, does it ever go away? The worry, do you get more relaxed about everything?” he asked Hodgson. “‘No chance, it’s impossible.’ I thought it would have been a little bit easier with age and experience. But in a way can’t help ourselves. I know what I want and the direction we should go in.”

Justin Cochrane – one of Thomas Tuchel’s assistants for England – has joined as first-team coach and took his first session with Palace on Monday less than 24 hours after the Nations League victory over Spain in Madrid. He is expected to be joined on Palace’s backroom staff by Bernardo Cueva, with Frank confirming that a deal with Chelsea is “very close” for the Mexican. Both worked with Frank at Brentford, where he spent almost nine years as an assistant and then manager. He is also hoping to add Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, who has been credited for his prowess on set-pieces: an area that Palace have struggled with for some time.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

But asked whether he will be judged on the perception that his success at Brentford was based on the model that has allowed his successor, Keith Andrews, to thrive since taking over, Frank was not impressed. “Put it this way, I think it was pretty important in terms of building that model,” he said.

#828. Claude, find me a planet: amateur astronomers are using AI with mixed results

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Artificial-intelligence tools are helping citizen scientists to find undiscovered exoplanets (artist’s illustration).Credit: Hypersphere/SPL

In September, Pavel Rabtsevich sat down at his computer and asked an AI model to discover a planet. Rabtsevich directed the bot to a specific batch of telescope data and gave it a high-level plan to hunt for evidence of undetected planets. In about two weeks, the bot delivered the goods: two possible planets orbiting a star 116 light years from Earth. Professional astronomers are now checking the bot’s findings.

History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI

History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI

Rabtsevich, who works in Spain as an artificial-intelligence specialist and has no formal astronomy education, is one of the most successful of a wave of amateur astronomers who are using AI models to search for worlds outside the Solar System. Citizen scientists have been using publicly available tools from NASA and other researchers to find planets for decades. But AI’s ability to scour the internet for such tools and use them to process massive amounts of data has lowered the barrier to entry for non-specialists who want to become planet hunters.

The newfound accessibility of data-analysis tools, however, has meant that not all amateurs are doing research responsibly, says Michelle Kunimoto, an exoplanet researcher at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada. Some planet hunters don’t fully understand the algorithms being used by AI tools and thus can’t validate the models’ findings, Kunimoto says. “There’s been a huge, overwhelming surge of AI-driven papers, which tend to have [planet] candidates that are not the best quality,” they say. And as a result, “the systems we use to disseminate science are being overwhelmed”.

For his search, Rabtsevich enlisted Claude Code, an AI coding tool made by Anthropic. He asked it to sift through data from more than 120,000 stars observed by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) in late 2025 and early 2026. He guided Claude to use a popular planet-detection algorithm to search for dips in the stars’ brightness. A regular and repeated dimming of a star can be a sign that a planet is orbiting it and blocking a little bit of light every time it passes between the star and an observer.

Claude zeroed in on a star called TIC 4206066 that showed two separate cycles of dimming, one roughly every 3 days and another every 11 days. That suggests that TIC 4206066 is orbited by two planets, one of which loops around the star more tightly than the other and thus takes less time to complete a full rotation.

These alien planets are astronomers’ favourites

These alien planets are astronomers’ favourites

Rabtsevich instructed Claude to look for those same repetitive patterns in archival TESS data. Sure enough, data from 2018 and 2020 recorded the same pattern of dimming coming from TIC 4206066. At Rabtsevich's direction, Claude then found a planet-detection algorithm, one written and made publicly available by Kunimoto, and ran it to validate the signals.

Rabtsevich published his findings to the platform Zenodo as a preprint1 on 25 September. His work has not been peer reviewed, but TESS astronomers have completed an independent analysis of the signals and have added them to their official list of planet candidates.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03790-w

#826. Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has said midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

#821. Stoke and Birmingham proving you shouldn't judge a book by its cover

Stoke's Jack McGlynn has scored in each of his past three games, while Blues' Jay Stansfield is on a run of three goals in two matches

Stoke City v Birmingham City: Third v first in the Championship.

That is a "tale of two cities" that did not look too likely to get written when Mark Robins' Potters started this season with three straight defeats and Blues won only two of their first eight league games under Chris Davies.

But, just like you should never judge a book by its cover, the footballing equivalent is to never judge any league table until after 10 games.

The season is now three months old - after Saturday's meeting at the Bet365 Stadium it will be more than a third of the way in.

And a clearer picture is starting to emerge as to whether what was once the "worst of times", especially in Stoke's case, might yet become the "best of times" before this 46-game campaign ends.

With 15 games gone, there are three clubs right at the top all on 29 points in what is already looking a ridiculously tight Championship table.

And two of them meet head on in front of an expected full house in the Potteries, having both been bang in form going into the latest international break.

Stoke are on a run of nine wins and only one defeat in 12 league games since the start of September, while Blues have won six out of seven since football returned after the first autumn international break.

So, how will things start to shape up after the second such break?

EFL preview: Evans' gripes & unexpected departures

Stoke had the edge last season, winning 1-0 at home in September before drawing 1-1 in the return at St Andrew's in January, prior to Blues going into their late-season decline - and Davies can see the difference in the Potters.

"I watched the game back from when we played them a year ago and it looks very different," the Blues boss told BBC Radio WM.

"He [Mark Robins] has made a big impact from where they were last season. A real stamp of his identity.

"They've gone to a back five and, since then, they've conceded the fewest goals in the league - nine in 12 games.

"They've looked strong, particularly in the central areas. They've got bigger. They're now one of the most physical starting XIs in the league."

While extolling the Potters' defensive qualities, Davies is also well aware they have an attacking threat and he is an admirer of Stoke's American winger Jack McGlynn, who is their top scorer with five goals.

"I already knew a little bit about the boy McGlynn," said Davies. "He's been exceptional with the goals he's got.

"They're a team much like ourselves. I want us to go there as a measure to see how far we've come, if we can display what we've been showing recently."

Mark Robins' Stoke and Birmingham City, under Chris Davies, have both recovered from dodgy starts to sit tied on 29 points

Stoke boss Mark Robins' main concern is determining the fitness of his international contingent, having had 10 out of his 20-man matchday squad from their 2-1 win at Portsmouth away for almost a fortnight.

Of the 14 players involved that day, Swedish keeper Viktor Johansson, Bosun Lawal (Ireland), Robert Bozenik (Slovenia), Luke Graham (Scotland) and euphoric Northern Ireland pair Ethan Galbraith and Justin Devenny all played, while McGlynn was part of new Manchester United boss Mauricio Pochettino's USA send-off.

"They've changed a little bit," Robins told BBC Midlands Today. "They've clearly taken a lot from the Championship last season.

"They've got some players in form and some coming back from international duty, although less than we have.

"A lot [of their players] have been together a few seasons now - and they've got some real talent. But it gives us a chance to pit ourselves against the team at the top. The last time we did that was against Charlton."

Having already seen off one table-topping team in the Potteries this season, Robins is not getting carried away though.

"It's nice to be where we are," he added. "We've never been in the conversation before and we want to be in that conversation."

Stoke will hold a minute's applause before the game to mark the recent passings of Potters legend Peter Dobing and former manager Gudjon Thordarson.

One local celebrity fan looking forward to Saturday's game more than most is a man with a foot in both camps - ex-Birmingham and Stoke full-back Ian Clarkson.

Boyhood Blues fan Clarkson made 174 appearances for the club between 1988 and 1993, when he moved on to Stoke, where he made a further 95 appearances.

After seeing out his career with Northampton Town, Kidderminster Harriers and Nuneaton Borough, Clarkson, now 55, then took his talents into the press box, reporting on Blues first for the Express & Star then the Birmingham Post - and he now coaches football in his teaching role at Repton College.

He has seen plenty of both clubs this season - and both have taken him slightly by surprise.

"Blues are a lot more inclined to attack than they were last season, they look more likely to take a few risks," Clarkson told BBC Sport.

"The signing of August Priske in January is obviously starting to reap rewards and it's bringing the best out of Jay Stansfield. Plus you've got good contributions coming from their wingers and two more on the bench to come on.

"Blues are playing some lovely football right now. Chris Davies is obviously a manager who works very hard at it. And they just seem to have got it right. They've clicked."

Ian Clarkson still sees a lot of Blues, working both as a BBC Radio WM summariser and some weeks as a St Andrew's matchday corporate host, a job he also does for the Potters

"Stoke are starting to look more like a Stoke City team, in the nicest possible way.

"Mark Robins is just one of those managers who, wherever he is, just seems to get better. The longer he stays at a club the better he gets. And they really do look far more resilient.

"There's something about the place that just feels different this season. They've got the fans back on side and that's more important than anything. Everyone knows how tough a place Stoke can be when it's bouncing."

As to who will win on Saturday? And where they might be come season's end?

"It's way too early to be talking in those terms," added Clarkson. "Let's be honest, I'm a Blues fan, so in any season I'd want Blues to finish top, then Stoke second. And they've both made great starts. But it's too soon to say. There's a long, long way to go."

#820. SFA should not change to pander to clubs - McLeish

Craig McLeish worked his way up from St Mirren's youth coaching ranks to become first-team manager

It is "damning" that Scottish FA chief football officer Craig Mulholland should have to "pander to clubs" as he attempts to bring in reforms, according to St Mirren manager Craig McLeish.

Mulholland and the SFA have engaged with Scottish Professional Football League clubs to encourage more playing time for younger players, but media speculation suggests those plans have been diluted.

And McLeish, who took over at St Mirren earlier this year, commented: "That's damning that he's having to change his plans to pander to clubs who aren't really on board with it and don't really have the best interests of the Scottish national team at heart.

"I understand why. We have owners from outwith this country. We have managers from outwith this country. They're in jobs, they're all fighting for their clubs.

"But why then are those people allowed to be the ones that hold the keys to the future of our country and the development of our national team?

"It's the way governance is set up and we've killed ourselves with that because the people who actually have a say in it have, not have no interest but they've got self-interest, and there's a lot of self-interest at the top end.

"I just don't see a way that we can really properly change unless something to do with governance changes and I just don't ever see that happening. It's really sad."

'Not fit for purpose' - Craig Mulholland on youth pathway

After reaching three of the past four major men's tournaments, Scotland struggled in their recent Nations League campaign, while Premiership clubs have missed out on the Champions League proper over the past two seasons.

The SFA had proposed including two under-21 players starting in cup competitions and the same age group playing a minimum of 6% of all available minutes across a season in league competition.

"We always focus at the top end, what our league size is, quotas for young players, a national base," 36-year-old McLeish, who worked in St Mirren's youth academy before his current role, said.

"We have a fundamental problem that starts at our youngest age groups, at four and five years of age, about how we actually teach kids to play. And, until you fix that, you can't fix the top end of it.

"It's crazy some of the stuff that's going on, the formats, how we teach kids. There's just a massive lack of education and expertise at the very bottom of our pathway.

"In this country, football's everyone's sport and everyone gets access to it, but if you take your young kids along to swimming or gymnastics or whatever other sport, you're there with properly qualified coaches, teachers who have maybe done things at the top levels of that sport.

"We have nothing without the volunteers that work at the bottom end of the grassroots game, but they're not teaching kids how to play football properly, in my mind.

"And you're just hoping that they get put with a volunteer coach that can teach them something, that they get in with a really good group at the youngest ages.

"Because that development between the ages of three and eight, if you don't get that right, you're dead. You can't do anything after that point and we don't do it well enough. And you're just chasing yourself and we'll never catch up."

Reporting McLeish's remarks, the Press Association said it had asked the SFA for comment.

They echo those of Dundee head coach Steven Pressley, who said on Thursday that Scotland would benefit from the creation of a national football centre and likened the current structure of the game to building on sand.

#819. Legendary Irish League manager Coyle dies aged 80

Coyle won 13 Irish League titles during an astonishing coaching career

Roy Coyle, the most successful manager in Irish League history, has died at the age of 80.

Coyle won 13 league titles during his 32-year managerial career, achieving periods of sustained success with Linfield and Glentoran.

He also managed Ards, Derry City and Newry City and had a spell as Glentoran director of football.

In a statement, Glentoran said the club were "deeply saddened to announce the passing of Roy Coyle, our former player and manager and one of the greatest figures in our history".

"A league champion in Glentoran colours, Roy went on to become the most successful manager in the club's history. His association with the Oval spanned more than half a century," their statement continued.

"His teams gave supporters some of their most treasured days, while his influence on players and colleagues endured long after his years in the dugout.

"To generations of the Glentoran family, he remained simply 'The Gaffer'."

A minute's silence will be held in Coyle's memory before Glentoran's Irish Premiership game against Cliftonville on Friday at Solitude.

Belfast native Coyle moved into management at the age of 29 when he was appointed player-manager of Linfield in November 1975.

A midfielder during his playing days, Coyle had spells with the Glens, Sheffield Wednesday, Grimsby Town and Linfield after starting out with Ballymena United, and he also won five caps for Northern Ireland.

During his 15 years as Blues boss, Coyle won 31 trophies, guiding the club to 10 league titles in just 12 seasons, alongside two Irish Cup successes and an All-Ireland crown in 1981.

"Everyone at Linfield Football Club is deeply saddened to learn of the passing of former player and manager, Roy Coyle," the club said.

"His remarkable achievements and contribution to one of the most successful periods in Linfield's history will forever be recognised and remembered.

"The thoughts and deepest condolences of everyone at Linfield Football Club are with Roy's family, friends and all who knew him at this sad time."

After his contract was terminated by Linfield in 1990, Coyle had a spell in the League of Ireland with Derry City between two stints at Ards.

In 1997, he took over at Glentoran and transformed their fortunes, leading the east Belfast club to three league titles and four Irish Cups.

Coyle went on to become the most successful in Glentoran's history, winning 17 trophies before his nine-year tenure at the Oval came to an end in 2006.

He had a brief period in charge of Newry City and also returned for three spells as caretaker boss of Glentoran before retiring in 2017.

Coyle retired from management in 2017 after his third spell as Glentoran interim manager

Glentoran chairman Colin Jess paid tribute to Coyle, who was inducted into the club's Hall of Fame in 2025.

"Roy was one of the greatest figures in Glentoran's history, and his passing is a profound loss for our club," said Jess.

"He gave generations of supporters some of the happiest days of their lives. People will always remember where they were and who they were with when his teams won those championships and cups. That is a wonderful thing to have given so many people.

"He set high standards and earned lasting respect. His former players continued to call him The Gaffer long after their playing days had ended, and that says so much about his influence and the place he held in their lives."

Jess added: "We will miss seeing Roy at the ground, enjoying his company and talking football with him. It is difficult to imagine the Oval without him.

"Our deepest sympathy goes to Abbie, the whole family and all those closest to Roy. We are immensely grateful for everything he gave Glentoran, and we will remember him with great affection and pride."

Glentoran owner Ali Pour described Coyle's contribution to Glentoran as "extraordinary".

"He helped make the club champions as a player, led it through years of success as manager and continued to serve it long afterwards," added Pour.

"I often asked Roy for his advice on matters at the club. He knew Glentoran so well, and I valued his judgement and hearing how he saw things. I'll miss those conversations.

"The pride with which supporters remember his teams, and the affection his former players have for him, show how deeply his work mattered to people.

"We owe Roy a great debt of gratitude. His achievements are an enduring part of Glentoran, and we will ensure that future generations understand what he gave this club and why he meant so much to it.

"My family and I extend our heartfelt condolences to Roy's family, friends and everyone mourning his loss. He will always have an honoured place at the Oval."

Northern Ireland Football League (NIFL) chief executive Gerard Lawlor said Coyle's contribution to football in Northern Ireland "went far beyond the trophies he won".

"He was a man who dedicated so much of his life to our local game, earning enormous respect across the football community, regardless of club loyalties," their statement continued.

"Roy represented the passion, commitment and pride that make Irish League football so special. His passing marks the loss of one of the great characters and personalities of our game, and his legacy will live on for generations."

Coyle, who started his playing career at Glentoran, won five caps for Northern Ireland

After taking over at Glentoran in 1997, Coyle became the club's most successful manager

Coyle lifted the Irish Cup four times as Glens boss

Coyle returned to the Glens dugout for three caretaker spells in 2012, 2015 and 2016

#818. Bella Hadid Cozies Up to Boyfriend Nathan Lacy During Aspen Trip

Bella Hadid enjoyed a shopping trip with her boyfriend Nathan Lacy in Aspen, Colo., on Nov. 17, with the couple showing off their romance with some sweet PDA.

Bella Hadid is getting cozy for cuffing season.

A week after hard launching her new romance with Nathan Lacy, the supermodel stepped out with her boyfriend for some vintage shopping in Aspen, Colo., on Nov. 17.

And the couple didn’t hold back on showing their love. Hadid and Lacy shared loving smooches and hugs, cuddling up together as they walked down the streets browsing the shops. In one sweet moment, the supermodel leaned her head on the construction worker's shoulders while he carried their shopping bags.

And though their romance is heating up, Hadid embodied chill vibes for the outing, bundling up in a white sweater with a denim jacket and matching denim jeans. Hadid—who styled her blonde locks in two pigtail braids—accessorized her winter look with a white beanie, black boots, cream gloves and a pair of black sunglasses.

As for Lacy, he sported a cream jacket over a blue plaid shirt, which he paired with dark jeans and sneakers.

But it wasn’t just the couple who enjoyed the shopping outing as they brought along their adorable golden retriever, which trotted along as Lacy walked it on a leash.

Though Hadid and Lacy first sparked romance rumors in September while on a grocery run together, it wasn’t until last week that the Victoria’s Secret Angel appeared to confirm the romance.

In a Nov. 9 Instagram post, the 30-year-old shed light on her and Lacy’s date night at a hockey game to watch the Colorado Avalanche beat the Detroit Red Wings on Nov. 7.

“Let’s go Avs!” Hadid wrote alongside the carousel of photos, which included PDA-filled shots with Lacy. “Saturday night was especially meaningful.”

And the Orabella founder emphasized that she loved cheering on the NHL team.

“I’ve always loved hockey living in NYC,” Hadid shared. “And being a Colorado girl at heart, growing up here since I was young, I guess it was only a matter of time before I found my way to the @coloradoavalanche.”

She added, “Regardless of where you are in the world—the heart, the grit, the camaraderie between teammates, the passion of the players, and the absolute die hard (in the best way) loyalty of the fans is the most epic thing to watch in real life when it comes to hockey!!!!”

#817. Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’

Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham

The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under‑21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one.

Time to talk, so let’s start with Tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field.

Hayworth’s family was from Seville province. “I know she was a great actress but I’m afraid I have to admit I’m not one for old films,” García concedes in an even tone. “My uncles played rugby for Ciencias and practically all of them were in the national team together. They tried to get me to play with my cousins, but I was always more into football.” He was good at it too: another Spain international, the Club World Cup’s top scorer, playing for Real Madrid.

Then this summer, with opportunities limited, he joined Fulham, his introductory interview conducted in impeccable English. Having joined Madrid aged 10, he was leaving home for the first time, as Fulham’s record signing, at 22. He had the language and intelligence to embrace it. As for being uprooted, he was used to that, growing up in Argentina and Chile as well as Spain.

“From very little my parents impressed upon me the importance of study, learning languages,” García says. “I’m at Villanueva university [in Madrid]. I started with dual honours business and analytics, although that became difficult with my profession. Now it’s just business, and I’m trying to arrange with the university how best to handle it [from London]. My parents considered it fundamental to speak English and I was always at international schools.

“Every two or three years we would change city. Obviously, there would be phases when I felt: ‘Pfff, again?!’ Having to move home because of my parents’ work. But I look back and feel grateful because, seen with perspective, it gives you opportunities to meet new people, see new places, learn. I’ve always had foreign friends with whom I spoke English.”

García has been joined at Fulham by César Palacios and Manuel Ángel from Madrid’s academy. Three 22-year-olds, like your very own Erasmus course. “Nah,” García says, laughing. “I wouldn’t call it an Erasmus because we’re talking about a big, ambitious career step. We’re grateful for the trust placed in us. I’ve been pleasantly surprised by London, a huge city with people from all nationalities and cultures and Fulham fit the situation I was in, the desire to grow.

“Álvaro Arbeloa explained the project, convinced me. I’d worked with him in Madrid. He knows me perfectly, how far he can push me. Equally, I know what he wants of me. That helps … [Arbeloa] told me it was a project that it will take time but that he needed me. I’m very, very happy. It’s one of the world’s best leagues, if not the best.”

And the toughest? Is English football as wild as it looks? “Yes!” García replies. “They had told me it was demanding, hard, but …” He cracks up. “I have to admit it still surprised me. That first game against Chelsea, I finished really, really tired. It was box to box, intense, a lot of running. Bit by bit I’m adapting. The intensity and pace is very different.

“Spain is more tactical, a bit more technical. English football is pace. You can’t lose concentration for a second, not a second. Anything can happen any moment. How many Premier League games are decided late? Suddenly there’s a goal in the 90th minute and again on 93. It’s your corner and their chance. The level of concentration, that constant transition, is what most sets the Premier League apart.”

Despite defeat on that opening day against Chelsea, García scored. A superb goal followed against AFC Wimbledon in the Carabao Cup. “It was super special to do it at Craven Cottage. I love how close the fans are – they can reach out and touch you. But I don’t consider myself someone who’s easily satisfied. I’m not like that. I always want more, more, more.”

García hasn’t scored since and Fulham went five league games without a win, pressure building. Which is where the calmness comes in. By the time they faced Hull, Arbeloa appeared on the edge of the sack, questions asked about his signings, García especially. Were three Madrid academy kids really what Fulham needed? Was the coach’s relationship with them not such a good thing after all?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

No player is impermeable to what is said, García admits, but he insists: “We treat that as outside noise. And we all knew that the beginning wouldn’t be easy. There’s a change of cycle: the coach goes, a new coach comes, there are signings, a different system, idea. Everyone has to adapt: those already at the club and those of us who are new. We’re young too. Results weren’t going our way but we had good intentions: to play good football, build, apply the manager’s ideas bit by bit. We had to remain calm.”

Fulham go into Saturday’s game at Manchester City unbeaten in four in the league, the sense of them shifting towards something more pragmatic not shared by García. “I don’t think we changed anything against Hull,” he says of a game Fulham won 1-0. “We didn’t do anything we weren’t already doing. Nothing. Maybe we controlled the small details that hurt us but the idea was the same. The players were very clear what the manager asked, very firm: it was just a question of time. You have to be patient. If you watch Fulham, you see the manager’s idea: have the ball, construct attacks well, show maximum intensity constantly with and without the ball. Aggressive, ambitious.”

Chances are coming for García but goals aren’t. He has started every league game but not scored or assisted since the opening day. Yet if there is a sense of a man feeling the pressure, that’s not repeated here; instead there’s an evenness, an ease. And a smile when another, more welcome, stat is raised: he has made more off‑the‑ball runs into the area than anyone. Something to hold on to, perhaps, a process that will pay off. “Really?” he says. “Well, I’m happy for people to see that a striker can help the team without the ball. In the end, it’s about following the manager’s instructions.”

In the end, though, teams will be judged on results and strikers on goals, price too. He knows: this is what he does, the path he chose. “Pressure depends on how you look at it, really,” García says. “Football is [very psychological]. It happens fast: it doesn’t give you time to enjoy good moments or linger on bad ones. It’s a rollercoaster – up there, down here. It’s not flat, but you maintain balance, work daily, improve: go in, focus, repeat.

“It’s not that I don’t ‘care’ about the price, it’s that the market is the market; it doesn’t depend on me. Calmness always, perspective … I know strikers are measured by goals but, well, the days I don’t score I’m completely sure I will be able to walk off the pitch and say that, no matter what happened, I helped my team, doing a load of other things. It is what it is.”

It is also time. A head peers around the door, the bus is going. García holds out a hand, apologises again. “It’s been a pleasure,” he says.

#816. EFL preview: Evans' gripes & unexpected departures

Steve Evans criticised his Bristol Rovers players last week after a disappointing 2-0 loss to Chesterfield left them 18th in the League Two table

The Championship resumes this weekend - but not all will be as it was.

Blackburn Rovers and Swansea City dip their feet into life without Tony Mowbray and Vitor Matos at their sides, for very different reasons.

Meanwhile, Bristol Rovers boss Steve Evans remains in charge in League Two but, given his comments after their last game, it might not be a relationship built to last.

Here are five things to capture your attention this EFL weekend.

Tony Mowbray (right) has left Blackburn Rovers in 13th place in the table while Vitor Matos (left) departs for France with Swansea City in sixth

It would have been a crushing blow to Blackburn fans to lose boss Mowbray, who stepped away due to ill health on Tuesday.

The veteran was surprising the league with a competitive Rovers side only three points away from the top eight and last registering a shock 2-1 win over big dogs West Ham United.

Rovers are not looking for an immediate successor and Mowbray may yet resume his managerial duties at some point, but the side will want to ensure they keep their fine form going rather than leaving him a salvage job to pull off should he return.

To do so, the team will have to put their concerns aside and focus on the job at hand - a Lancashire derby with struggling Burnley at Turf Moor on Sunday (12:00 GMT).

But they are not the only team to be without their trusty manager.

Matos has spread his wings to fly over to Strasbourg and leaves his Swans in a healthy league position but also in poor form.

The Welsh side have lost four of their past five (W1) to begin falling down the pecking order but still remain inside the play-off places, three points below the league leaders and three above West Ham in ninth.

Matos has taken four members of his coaching staff with him, meaning former Swans players Joe Allen and Ashley Williams have stepped in as a makeshift coaching set-up before a difficult game against fifth-placed West Bromwich Albion on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

"Swansea were doing great but I felt they were performing at their absolute maximum," former Stoke full-back Tommy Smith told the 72+ podcast this week.

"I think it's a good opportunity for him, a good opportunity for Strasbourg but it's a tough one for Swansea to take."

Swansea's summer signings 'let down' by Matos

Millwall have won their past three home fixtures against London rivals QPR

Queens Park Rangers boss Julien Stephan believes their London derby against Millwall on Saturday lunchtime (12:30 GMT) will be the first of five games to truly define his side.

The R's are going strong so far this season. They sit inside the play-off positions, five points off the league leaders but it's not enough yet to convince everyone they have finally become promotion contenders after 12 years mostly in the doldrums.

"The thing that is going to hold us back is consistency," QPR fan Gareth Dixon told BBC Radio London.

"We have far too many players injured too frequently. Getting that first, strongest XI is a challenge for us.

"If we can get our strongest team out, if we can keep the performances up then we are looking at top eight."

Millwall, meanwhile, know what it's like to push for a place in the Premier League in recent times, but things have not panned out so well this season.

Injuries have hampered them and after only two wins in their past 10 league games, both against teams in the bottom three, the Lions' season is yet to really get going.

All three of the Championship clubs based in the West Midlands plus Staffordshire's Stoke City are within one point of each other at the top of the table

There is something in the air around the western side of the Midlands.

Only Middlesbrough disrupt a top five of West Midlands and Staffordshire clubs and the two best of that bunch are league leaders Birmingham City and third-placed Stoke City.

Both are on three-match winning streaks and sit on 29 points, separated merely by Blues' superior goal difference.

Saturday's game at the Bet365 Stadium (15:00 GMT) will see the two go head-to-head for a top-two spot - and possibly top spot itself.

But a draw could open the door for either Wolves or West Bromwich Albion to reach the summit instead.

I mean, just look how tight the division is.

Dave Challinor was announced as new Sheffield Wednesday boss on 1 November

In a game against fellow promotion contenders Plymouth Argyle last weekend, Sheffield Wednesday claimed a convincing 3-0 victory to mark Dave Challinor's return to League One management.

Their next opponent, Barnsley, seem like they will be an easier ride. The Tykes have the joint fewest points in the league with nine, kept off the bottom through goal difference alone.

A derby under the lights can produce something special though.

Barnsley have won both their previous matches against Wednesday and will be seeking a third in a row for the first time since 1946.

No one is expecting the Tykes to claim all three points when they meet on Friday night (20:00 GMT) but that means all the pressure is on the rebuilding Wednesday side.

The Owls did not deal so well with that expectation in the two cup games Challinor began his reign with, losing in the FA Cup to Oldham Athletic and suffering a 4-0 drubbing in the EFL Trophy against Accrington Stanley.

Can they rise to the occasion or is it Barnsley's time to get motoring?

Challinor hoping Argyle win is just 'the start'

Few bosses in League Two have the experience of Steve Cotterill and Steve Evans

Cheltenham Town boss Steve Cotterill isn't much loved by the Bristol Rovers fan base.

The 62-year-old led the Gas' local rivals Bristol City to the League One title and the EFL Trophy in 2015, earning the Robins' eternal admiration and Rovers' unrelenting dislike.

However, back at his boyhood club, Cotterill will be aiming to quieten his critics among the away support as he looks to take Cheltenham into the League Two play-off spots when the two sides face each other on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

His current Robins have lost five of their past seven games (W2) but still remain just a point shy of the top seven.

Rovers, meanwhile, are tumbling down the table at a rapid rate after a seven-game winless run where they have taken just one point - and they are hardly putting up a united front.

Manager Steve Evans has suggested he will depart the club if he feels they no longer want his services and has placed blame on his players for their run of poor form.

"You're going to Steve Cotterill's Cheltenham side, who are very good, particularly at Whaddon Road," Evans told BBC Radio Bristol after their loss to Chesterfield last weekend.

"We have to pick a team first and foremost that works hard and fights.

"I'll still turn up at 6.30 in the morning. I'll still leave at 6 o'clock at night. I still go and watch the opposition, do the analysis. What's changed? I know what's changed â inconsistent players."

You can follow the entire EFL weekend as it happens here on the BBC Sport website and app, starting with live text coverage of Barnsley v Sheffield Wednesday on Friday, 20 November.

#815. Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden

The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly

It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it.

But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. It’s just a noise, but it’s unmistakably Danny Kelly. He regains the power of speech and follows it up with: “Gooooaaaal … Goalll Stan, Goalll at the Emirates.” Reporter Ian Abrahams and Stan Collymore join the excitement, before Danny comes back: “I LOVE FOOTBALL, STAN, I LOVE IT.” It is such a brilliant piece of radio. From one of the absolute greats.

Danny died last week. In a beautiful tribute on the Spurs podcast he hosted – A View From the Lane – Charlie Eccleshare pointed out the irony that for someone so articulate and erudite and able to do so much more than just “the football”, his most iconic moment is so simple. Even the opening noise – not even a real word – is perfect in that context.

Terms such as pioneer and trailblazer often get thrown out in moments like this. But Danny really was. I first met him at BBC London more than 20 years ago. As someone who’d listened to him and Danny Baker as a teenager, I couldn’t really believe I was in the same office as them. His career was ridiculous, editing the NME and Q magazine, setting up Football365, but it was radio where I knew him. He understood the absurdity of life and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living by talking about football. I remember at TalkSport one World Cup – 2018 perhaps – wandering in and he was hosting a live match, watching a game on the TV just marvelling at the fact that this was a job, and that this was his job.

And he was funny. Blimey he was funny – what an ability to be blessed with. I listened to a best of Baker and Kelly Upfront from the old Radio 5 on YouTube the other day; amazing calls about Arthur Cox locking a disgruntled fan in his office for two and a half hours, a man playing football with a pig’s head in a sausage factory in Peckham: “I used to like the volleys when the eyes popped out.” Anyone who has tried to make funny football content, of any kind – radio, TV, podcasts, social media – owes him a debt of gratitude.

Last Wednesday Charlie Baker and I had to try to do him justice on TalkSport. Afternoon UK time, midnight till 3am for me in Australia. I was asleep when my phone rang and instantly presumed I’d slept through my alarm and missed the show. A millisecond of internal panic surged through me as I jumped up and cracked a shin on the bedside table. Danny would appreciate the ridiculous scene of me hopping around in the dark trying not to wake the kids while one of the bosses gave me the incredibly sad news.

If you’ve broadcast for any amount of time, you will be confronted with having to host shows just after someone has died. Jack Charlton, Terry Venables, Jimmy Greaves – but never before have I had to pay tribute to a friend.

Paul Hawksbee’s voice cracks and we all go. There are West Ham and Chelsea fans calling admitting they listen to his Spurs podcast because it’s him. There are all manner of texts recounting hilarious stories they heard on his shows over the last 30 years: the man who took a TV to a game in Northern Ireland so they could watch the FA Cup final, having to move around holding the aerial to keep the signal.

There’s a moment I think Danny would have found so funny, when I’m being sad – because it is sad, and I am sad – and into the break I read the sponsor’s lines: “This show is brought to you by Toolstation, first stop Toolstation” in such a maudlin way it’s as if I’m delivering a eulogy, just one sponsored by a hardware store. I catch myself just in time.

But, most important, there are so many messages from people who never met Danny, who never knew him, but who felt as if they knew him. We believed he would have wanted a bit of fuss made of him.

He definitely knew the enduring power of radio, even as the broadcasting landscape changes so quickly. It connects in a way nothing else can. And nothing said that more than messages we received from listeners who at one time or another were struggling and going through incredibly hard times and Danny’s energy, wit and joy were an escape and a tonic.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There will be a million people more important in Danny’s life than me. Our paths crossed a great deal, but never for very long. I was a minuscule cog in his world – but Danny had so much love to give. Voice notes about how to broadcast remotely or celebrating Spurs’ win in Bilbao; the tributes showed he had almost infinite time for others.

It always feels such a bland cliche to say it’s impossible to consider someone so full of life not being there – we all know we have a sell-by date. At the start of October he had been given a choice: to ebb away slowly over a couple of years or have a big but very risky operation. Danny never ebbed.

He sent a big group WhatsApp voice note to many friends and colleagues, and I don’t think he would mind me writing what it said.

“I want you to know that I’ve enjoyed being around you, I’ve learnt from you, I’ve enjoyed working with you, you know how much I love my work – the fact I’m pretty good at it is secondary to how much I enjoy it, but look I’m very much hopeful that the boffins and my own determination will get me through this and we can all laugh about this message. But know how I care about you, how much you have meant in my life and on Thursday night or Friday morning when you look at the sky or feel the wind against your face, think about me and what’s happening and hopefully we’ll all have a pint and a laugh about this somewhere down the line.”

From “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH” to that – his words just hit the right tone every time.

#814. Why Kacey Musgraves, Miranda Lambert Song Cut Out at CMA Awards

During Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert’s performance of “Horses and Divorces” at the CMA Awards 2026, their vocals were partially cut from broadcast. Here’s why.

Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert might like to cuss (and smoke and drink) but the CMA Awards had reign them in.

During the duo’s rendition of their song “Horses and Divorces” at the CMA Awards Nov. 18, many country fans noticed that their performance was partially obstructed from the broadcast—and that’s all due to the language in the song.

While some stars opt to perform a clean version of their songs to follow the Federal Communications Commission guidelines, Musgraves and Lambert performed the original lyrics, which sees Lambert sing, “I’ve done my fair share of s--t talkin,’ too.”

Those present at the ceremony in Bridgestone Arena in Nashville were able to hear Lambert’s entire vocals, but during the ABC broadcast, there was a few seconds of white noise that confused viewers—especially those unfamiliar with the duet.

Luckily, the country singers’ hook, “hell just froze over” is permitted by the FCC and it exemplifies just how momentous the song—which is featured on Musgraves’ album Middle of Nowhere—truly is, considering the stars were previously at odds which each other.

Musgraves admitted during an interview with CBS Mornings earlier this year that it was “common knowledge there was a bit of soft tension” between her and Lambert—and so she decided to bury the hatchet once and for all by featuring the “The House that Built Me” singer on her latest album.

Lambert, for her part, shared she was surprised by Musgraves’ request.

“I hadn’t heard from her in a while,” Lambert—who split from Blake Shelton in 2015—explained in a separate interview during the same CBS Mornings segment. “She texted me and was like, ‘I need to ask you something but I need to ask you on the phone, like I want to talk about this.’”

Musgraves—whose breakup with husband Ruston Kelly occurred five years later in 2020—noted that while she was putting together her album, she saw a video of Lambert riding her horse online and thought, “‘Hey, at least we’ve got two things in common.’”

And so, she thought of the concept for “Horses and Divorces.” When Musgraves pitched the song to Lambert, now married to Brendan McLoughlin, and said “we need to write it,” the 43-year-old said she was immediately game, saying, “Hell yeah we do.”

As she put it, “It was an immediate yes.”

For more of what you might have missed at the CMA Awards, keep reading…

#813. Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'

Mykhailo Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine

Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.

Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.

In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.

He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample.

"The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work."

He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.

In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.

However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty.

And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words".

"Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added.

"These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.

"The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.

"I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism.

"If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question."

BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.

#812. Germany gives sweeping powers to police, intelligence services

Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic and foreign sources?

Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday.

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Germany's foreign intelligence service, will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany.

Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies.

Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The president of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch this week again pointed out that today's hybrid attacks pose a new challenge to the organizations safeguarding the country's security. At his organization's annual meeting in Berlin this week, he said the "hybrid attacks" are challenging the "separation principle," which means that the police conduct investigations while intelligence services gather information. The exchange of data between the two is permitted only under strict conditions.

Münch has long objected to this strict division of responsibilities. He has been calling for expanded powers for the police and closer cooperation with the domestic intelligence agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which is responsible for countering espionage and sabotage.

The separation principle results from lessons learned from the Nazi dictatorship, when the Secret State Police (Gestapo) operated largely outside judicial constraints and served as the regime's central instrument of terror, used to oppress and murder Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, communists, social democrats and many others. The Allied powers that defeated Nazi Germany in World War II then decided that the police and intelligence services should remain institutionally separate and be granted different powers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Historian Sönke Neitzel of the University of Potsdam considers the separation principle understandable in its historical context. At the BKA's autumn conference, however, he described it as "nonsense" in light of today's threat landscape and said it was no longer necessary in a country that has been a constitutional democracy for decades.

While Neitzel considers the separation principle outdated, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the center-right Christian Social Union (CSU) wants to preserve it in its essential form. In his view, even a more extensive exchange of data does not violate the principle. At the same time, however, he has made clear that he wants to transform the domestically focused Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the BND into "real intelligence services."

This legislative reform brings Dobrindt a significant step closer to that goal. Parliament approved the interior minister's plans with the votes of the governing coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dobrindt insisted that Germany intends to take an active approach to defending itself against cyberattacks: "Anyone who attacks us in this way must know that we are prepared to strike back. They must know that their digital infrastructure, their server infrastructure, and their software will also be targeted by us."

BKA President Holger Münch welcomes Dobrindt's determination and points to the growing threat posed by cyberattacks. The line between criminal and state-sponsored actors is becoming increasingly blurred, he argues. As a result, both intelligence services and law enforcement agencies face the same challenge.

To underscore the scale of the threat as he sees it, Münch cited two statistics: in the first six months of 2026, crime originating from abroad rose by 24% compared with the same period the previous year. What concerns him most is that fewer than 5% of these cases are solved. The BKA chief considers this trend more dangerous than ever: "The state's promise of security can become fragile. Confidence in the ability of its institutions to act effectively and remain steadfast is declining."

This article was originally written in German.
